Chapter 1Points, Lines, and the Art of Definition

✦ Wonder

Try to define the word “point” to a friend, using only simpler words. Then define those words. Keep going. You will find, surprisingly quickly, that you run out of simpler words entirely. Where does a chain of definitions begin?

Every dictionary is secretly a circle. Look up “line” and it sends you to “straight”; look up “straight” and it sends you back to “line.” For ordinary language this is harmless. For mathematics, where we demand certainty, it is a crisis — because if our definitions chase each other in circles, our proofs rest on nothing. The Greeks found the only possible escape, and it is the foundation of everything that follows.

The terms we agree not to define

We choose a tiny handful of words and agree, openly, not to define them. Instead we describe how they behave. These are the primitive (or undefined) terms. In plane geometry there are just three: a point marks a position with no size; a line is straight, thin, and endless in both directions; a plane is a perfectly flat surface extending forever.

Aha!

We do not build mathematics by defining everything. We build it by defining almost everything in terms of a few honest, undefined starting points — and then never sneaking in a hidden assumption again. Knowing where to stop defining is the first act of mathematical maturity.

From these three primitives, every other object is built by definition. For distinct points A and B: the segment AB is A, B, and all points between (finite); the ray →AB starts at A and runs through B forever (one endpoint and a direction); the line through them extends forever both ways. The length of AB is written AB.

The rules of the game: a first axiom

An axiom is a statement we accept as true without proof — a rule of the game agreed at the start. Everything we prove traces back to axioms. The first captures something you have always known.

Axiom · Two-Point

Through any two distinct points there passes exactly one line.

It says two things at once: you can always draw a line through two points (“at least one”), and you can never draw two different ones (“at most one”). That uniqueness is what lets “the line AB” name a single, definite object. Points are collinear if one line passes through all of them; lines are concurrent if one point lies on all of them.

✗ Common Trap

“Two lines always meet at a point.” Not so! Two lines in a plane either meet at exactly one point or never meet at all. Lines that never meet are parallel — the subject of an entire chapter (Chapter 3).

Distance, betweenness, and the midpoint

A line is more than a set of points: along it we can measure. The everyday fact that the whole equals the sum of its parts becomes, on a line, a working axiom.

Theorem · Segment Addition

If B lies between A and C on a line, then AB + BC = AC. Conversely, if AB+BC=AC, then B lies between A and C.

A point that splits a segment into two equal halves is its midpoint: M is the midpoint of AB when AM = MB = ½AB.

☞ Worked Example

Point B lies between A and C, with AB=7 and AC=12. Find BC.

By Segment Addition, AB+BC=AC, so BC = AC−AB = 12−7 = 5. The whole (12) minus the part you have (7) leaves the rest (5). ■

☞ Worked Example

M is the midpoint of AB, with AM = 3x−1 and MB = x+5. Find AB.

A midpoint makes the two halves equal, so AM=MB:

3x−1 = x+5  ⇒  2x = 6  ⇒  x = 3.

Then AM = 3(3)−1 = 8, and since AB is two halves, AB = 2·AM = 16. (Check: MB = x+5 = 8 too.) Geometry has quietly become a one-line equation — a foreshadowing of Chapter 21. ■

Why this much care?

It may feel excessive to fuss over the word “point.” But this care is the price of certainty, and it pays for itself at once: because our terms are pinned down, the next time we write “let ℓ be the line through A and B,” there is no ambiguity, no hidden assumption, no crack for an error to slip through.

☞ Worked Example

How many lines are determined by 5 points, if no three of them are collinear?

Each line is fixed by choosing 2 of the points (the Two-Point Axiom), and since no three are collinear, different pairs give different lines. The number of ways to choose 2 of 5 is

C(5,2) = 5·42 = 10.

So exactly 10 lines. The phrase “no three collinear” does real work: without it, three points on one line would be counted as three pairs but give only one line. ■

➤ Your turn

At a party of 9 people, everyone shakes hands exactly once with everyone else. How many handshakes take place?

Set-up (you finish it): a handshake is a choice of 2 people from 9 — the same count as the segments joining 9 points with no three collinear. So evaluate C(9,2) = (9·8)/2.

Answer: C(9,2) = 36 handshakes.

We spent a whole chapter learning where to stop asking “but what is that?”, and on that small patch of bedrock everything else in this book will stand.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Primitives (undefined): point, line, plane — described by behaviour, not defined.
  • Built objects: segment AB (finite), ray →AB (one endpoint + direction), line (infinite); AB = length.
  • Two-Point Axiom: exactly one line through two distinct points.
  • Collinear points share a line; concurrent lines share a point.
  • Segment Addition: B between A,C ⇒ AB+BC=AC; the midpoint gives AM=MB=½AB.
  • Counting: n points, no three collinear, determine C(n,2) = n(n−1)/2 lines.

Chapter 2Angles and How to Measure Them

✦ Wonder

The hour hand of a clock creeps from 12 all the way around back to 12. The minute hand does the same in one hour; the second hand, in one minute. All three return to where they began — yet we feel that the second hand has “turned more.” What exactly is the thing that is being measured when something turns?

That “thing” is the angle: the measure of turning, or equivalently of the opening between two directions. It is the single most important quantity in elementary geometry. Master angles and you hold the key to triangles, circles, and — as Part IV will show — to half of all olympiad problems.

The anatomy of an angle

Definition · Angle

An angle is the figure formed by two rays sharing a common endpoint. The shared endpoint is the vertex; the two rays are the sides. The angle with vertex V and sides through A and B is written ∠AVB (or ∠BVA, or simply ∠V when there is no ambiguity).

The middle letter always names the vertex — a small convention with a big payoff in crowded diagrams.

Measuring the turn: degrees

To measure an angle we compare it to a full turn. Slice one complete revolution into 360 equal parts and call each part one degree, written 1°. Then a full turn is 360°, a half-turn is 180°, and a quarter-turn is 90°.

Mathematician’s Margin

Why 360, and not a rounder number like 100? The choice descends from the Babylonians, who used a base-60 number system and reckoned a year at about 360 days. The number 360 is also gloriously divisible — by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12 and more — so most natural fractions of a turn come out whole. We keep it out of a four-thousand-year-old habit, and because it is genuinely convenient.

Angles earn names by their size. Commit these to memory; we will use them constantly.

The right angle is special enough to deserve its own mark: a small square at the vertex, never an arc. When two lines meet at a right angle we say they are perpendicular, written ℓ ⊥ m.

Angles that add

If a ray VC lies in the interior of ∠AVB, then it splits the big angle into two smaller ones that must account for the whole. This is the Angle Addition Postulate:

∠AVB = ∠AVC + ∠CVB.

Obvious? Yes. Useful? Endlessly — it is the engine of every “angle chase” you will ever run, and the reason the simple act of drawing one extra ray so often cracks a problem open.

A ray that splits an angle into two equal parts is its bisector. Two other relationships appear so often they are named:

Definition · Complementary and supplementary

Two angles are complementary if their measures sum to 90°, and supplementary if they sum to 180°. When two angles are supplementary and share a side, forming a straight line, they are a linear pair.

☞ Worked Example

Ray VC bisects ∠AVB, with ∠AVC = (2x+5)° and ∠CVB = (3x−10)°. Find ∠AVB.

A bisector makes the two halves equal, so ∠AVC = ∠CVB:

2x+5 = 3x−10  ⇒  x = 15.

Then ∠AVC = 2(15)+5 = 35°, and by Angle Addition ∠AVB = 2·35° = 70°. (Check: ∠CVB = 3(15)−10 = 35° too.) ■

☞ Worked Example

Find the angle that is exactly twice its own complement.

Let the angle be x; its complement is 90°−x, and we want x = 2(90°−x):

x = 180° − 2x  ⇒  3x = 180°  ⇒  x = 60°.

So the angle is 60° and its complement is 30° — and indeed 60 is twice 30. Naming a relationship turned a sentence of English into a one-line equation. ■

Your first theorem: vertical angles

When two lines cross, they make four angles. The two that sit “across” from each other — sharing only the vertex — are called vertical angles. Your eye insists they are equal. Let us prove it, and feel for the first time the difference between seeing and knowing.

Theorem · Vertical Angle Theorem

If two lines intersect, then vertical angles are equal. In the figure, ∠1 = ∠3.

Proof. Angles 1 and 2 form a linear pair, so ∠1 + ∠2 = 180°. Angles 2 and 3 also form a linear pair, so ∠2 + ∠3 = 180°. Setting these equal,

∠1 + ∠2 = ∠2 + ∠3.

Subtract ∠2 from both sides: ∠1 = ∠3. The same argument gives ∠2 = ∠4. ■

Aha!

Look at what just happened. We did not measure a single angle. We never appealed to the picture. We used only the meaning of “linear pair” and ordinary arithmetic — and out came a fact that holds for every pair of crossing lines that ever has been or will be drawn. That is the power you are here to learn.

☞ Worked Example

Two lines cross. One of the four angles measures 35°. Find the other three.

Its vertical partner is also 35°. Each of the remaining two forms a linear pair with the 35° angle, so each is 180° − 35° = 145°. The four angles are 35°, 145°, 35°, 145° — and indeed they go around the point summing to 360°.

☞ Worked Example · Back to the clock

What is the angle between the hour and minute hands at exactly 4:00?

The twelve hour-marks split the full 360° into twelve equal steps of 30°. At 4:00 the minute hand points at 12 and the hour hand at 4, a gap of four steps:

4 × 30° = 120°.

So the hands make 120° — the Wonder’s vague feeling of “how much turning” is now a number you compute from a fraction of a full revolution. (Beware the moving hour hand at times like 4:30.) ■

➤ Your turn

Two angles are supplementary, and one of them is exactly four times the other. Find both angles.

Set-up (you finish it): call the smaller angle x; the larger is 4x, and “supplementary” means x + 4x = 180°. Solve for x, then check the two add to 180°.

Answer: x = 36° and 4x = 144° (and 36 + 144 = 180).

What began as the second hand’s vague feeling of “more turning” is now a quantity you can measure, add, and reason with — and you proved your very first theorem along the way.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Angle: two rays from a vertex; written ∠AVB (middle letter = vertex). Measured in degrees; a full turn = 360°.
  • Names: acute <90°, right =90° (perpendicular, ⊥), obtuse 90°–180°, straight =180°, reflex >180°.
  • Angle Addition: an interior ray gives ∠AVB = ∠AVC + ∠CVB; a bisector halves an angle.
  • Complementary sum to 90°; supplementary sum to 180°; a linear pair is supplementary and straight.
  • Vertical angles (from two crossing lines) are equal — proved from two linear pairs.

Chapter 3Parallel Lines and the Transversal

✦ Wonder

Railway tracks run side by side, never meeting, all the way to the horizon — and yet in a photograph they appear to converge to a single point. Are the rails “really” parallel, or do our eyes know something our rulers do not? And if two lines truly never meet, the angles around them are no longer free; they fall into a strict and beautiful lockstep.

Parallel lines are where geometry first becomes genuinely surprising. Two lines that never touch, no matter how far you follow them, turn out to impose strict, beautiful rules on every angle in their neighbourhood. Those rules are the heartbeat of the angle chase — the technique that will carry you to the olympiad.

What “parallel” means

Definition · Parallel lines

Two lines in the same plane are parallel if they never meet, however far they are extended. We write ℓ ∥ m.

A line that cuts across two (or more) other lines is called a transversal. When a transversal crosses two lines it creates eight angles — four at each crossing — and these come in families with names worth learning.

The vocabulary, all referring to the figure: corresponding angles sit in matching corners at the two crossings — the pairs (1,5), (2,6), (3,7), (4,8); think of the letter F. Alternate interior angles lie between the two lines on opposite sides of t — (3,6) and (4,5); think of the letter Z. Co-interior (same-side interior) angles lie between the lines on the same side — (3,5) and (4,6); think of the letter C.

The Parallel Postulate, in working form

Here is the axiom that makes everything go — the modern, practical face of Euclid’s famous fifth postulate.

Axiom · Corresponding Angles

A transversal cuts two lines so that a pair of corresponding angles are equal if and only if the two lines are parallel.

The phrase “if and only if” means the street runs both ways: parallel lines force corresponding angles to be equal, and equal corresponding angles guarantee the lines are parallel. The second direction is how we will later prove that two lines are parallel — by catching a pair of equal angles. From this single axiom, the other two families follow as theorems.

Theorem · Alternate Interior Angles

If ℓ ∥ m, then alternate interior angles are equal: ∠3 = ∠6.

Proof. Since ℓ ∥ m, corresponding angles are equal, so ∠3 = ∠7. But ∠7 and ∠6 are vertical angles, so ∠7 = ∠6. Chaining these, ∠3 = ∠7 = ∠6. ■

Theorem · Co-interior Angles

If ℓ ∥ m, then co-interior angles are supplementary: ∠3 + ∠5 = 180°.

Proof. Angles 3 and 6 are alternate interior, so ∠3 = ∠6. Angles 6 and 5 form a linear pair, so ∠6 + ∠5 = 180°. Substituting, ∠3 + ∠5 = 180°. ■

☞ Worked Example

Lines ℓ ∥ m are cut by a transversal, and one of the eight angles is 70°. Find the angle that is (a) corresponding to it, (b) alternate interior to it, (c) co-interior with it.

Corresponding angles are equal, so (a) is 70°. Alternate interior angles are equal, so (b) is 70°. Co-interior angles are supplementary, so (c) is 180°−70° = 110°. Two of the three relationships preserve the angle; only the co-interior one flips it to its supplement. ■

☞ Worked Example

A transversal makes a pair of co-interior angles measuring (2x+20)° and (3x+10)°. For what x are the two lines parallel?

Run the axiom in reverse: the lines are parallel exactly when co-interior angles are supplementary, so we require

(2x+20) + (3x+10) = 180  ⇒  5x+30 = 180  ⇒  x = 30.

At x=30 the angles are 80° and 100° (summing to 180°), so the lines are parallel. This is the everyday way parallelism is proved — catch an angle relationship and quote the converse. ■

Aha!

Notice the pattern of the last two proofs: we never started from scratch. We borrowed a fact we had already secured (corresponding angles, vertical angles, linear pairs) and took one more step. This is how all of geometry is built — each theorem standing on the shoulders of the ones before. You are watching a tower rise.

✗ Common Trap

The neat equalities hold only when the two lines are parallel. If ℓ and m are not parallel, corresponding angles are simply unequal and carry no special relationship. Always confirm the parallel marks before you use these rules.

A trick worth its weight in gold: the auxiliary parallel

Here is a problem that looks impossible until one extra line makes it trivial — your first taste of the single most powerful move in olympiad geometry: adding a helpful line.

☞ Worked Example

Two horizontal lines are parallel. A point P lies between them. A segment runs from the upper line down to P, making an angle of a with the upper line; another runs from P down to the lower line, making an angle of b with the lower line, on the opposite side. Show that the bend at P equals a+b.

The idea: draw a third line through P parallel to the two given lines. It splits the bend angle at P into two pieces. The upper piece and a are alternate interior angles between two parallels, so the upper piece = a. The lower piece and b are likewise alternate interior, so the lower piece = b. By the Angle Addition Postulate, the whole bend is the sum of its pieces:

∠P = a + b.  ■
Aha!

Keep this manoeuvre close. When a configuration involves parallel lines and a stubborn angle, the question to ask is almost always: “what if I drew one more line parallel to those?” Half of beginning olympiad geometry is knowing which line to add.

➤ Your turn

Lines ℓ ∥ m are cut by a transversal, and a pair of alternate interior angles measures (2x+15)° and (4x−25)°. Find x and the size of each angle.

Set-up (you finish it): alternate interior angles across parallels are equal, so set 2x+15 = 4x−25, solve for x, then substitute back.

Answer: x = 20, and each angle is 2(20)+15 = 55°.

Two lines that agree never to meet end up dictating every angle in sight — and one well-chosen extra line unlocks them. You have just met the move that runs through all of olympiad geometry.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Parallel (ℓ ∥ m): lines that never meet. A transversal crossing them makes eight angles.
  • Corresponding (F) angles equal iff the lines are parallel — true both ways.
  • Alternate interior (Z) angles equal; co-interior (C) angles supplementary (sum 180°).
  • Each has a converse used to prove two lines parallel — catch the angle relationship, quote the converse.
  • Auxiliary parallel: through a troublesome point draw a line parallel to the given ones; alternate-interior angles then split the mystery angle into nameable pieces.

Chapter 4Triangles and the 180° Miracle

✦ Wonder

Draw any triangle you like — long and thin, squat and wide, perfectly even. Tear off its three corners and lay them side by side, tip to tip. Every time, without exception, they fit together into a perfectly straight line. A skinny triangle, a fat triangle, a triangle the size of a galaxy: always a straight line. Why should three angles that look nothing alike always add up to the very same total?

The triangle is the most important shape in all of geometry. It is the simplest figure that encloses space, the unit from which every polygon can be built, and the stage on which nearly every theorem you will ever prove first appears. And it guards a remarkable secret, the one your torn corners just revealed.

The triangle, defined

Definition · Triangle

A triangle is the figure formed by three points, not all collinear, joined in pairs by segments. The three points are its vertices, the three segments its sides, and the angles at the vertices its interior angles. The triangle with vertices A, B, C is written △ABC.

The condition “not all collinear” matters: three points on one line give no triangle at all, just a flattened segment.

The angle-sum theorem

Theorem · Angle Sum

The three interior angles of any triangle sum to 180°.

Before the proof, savour the strategy, because it is a perfect example of the auxiliary-line idea from Chapter 3. The angles of the triangle are scattered at three different vertices — hard to compare. We will use one cleverly drawn parallel line to transport all three angles to a single point, where they visibly line up.

Proof. Let the interior angles at A, B, C be α, β, γ. Through the vertex C, draw the line ℓ parallel to the opposite side AB. The side CA is a transversal cutting the parallels, so the angle it makes with ℓ on the left equals α (alternate interior angles); likewise CB makes an angle equal to β on the right. Now the three angles at C — the transported α, the original γ, and the transported β — together fill the straight line ℓ. Angles on a straight line sum to 180°, so

α + γ + β = 180°.  ■
Aha!

The triangle’s three angles were never really independent. The parallel line revealed that they are simply the three pieces of a single straight angle, broken apart and carried to different corners. The “miracle” was a straight line in disguise all along.

An immediate harvest

One theorem, proved well, pays dividends at once. Here is a corollary we get almost for free, itself a workhorse of angle chasing.

Theorem · Exterior Angle

If one side of a triangle is extended, the exterior angle so formed equals the sum of the two remote (non-adjacent) interior angles.

Proof. Extend side AB beyond B to a point D. The exterior angle ∠CBD and the interior angle β = ∠CBA form a linear pair, so ∠CBD = 180° − β. But by the angle-sum theorem α + γ = 180° − β as well. Therefore ∠CBD = α + γ. ■

☞ Worked Example

An exterior angle of a triangle measures 130°, and the two remote interior angles are equal. Find all three interior angles.

The exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles. With those two equal to x each, 2x = 130°, so x = 65°. The third interior angle (adjacent to the exterior one) is 180°−130° = 50°. (Check: 65+65+50 = 180.) The exterior angle did the work in one step. ■

A family portrait: classifying triangles

Triangles are sorted in two independent ways — by their angles and by their sides.

These two classifications interact in ways worth noticing: a triangle can be right and isosceles, but — as the angle-sum theorem quietly guarantees — never obtuse and equilateral. (An equilateral triangle’s angles are all equal, hence each is 180°/3 = 60°, all acute.)

☞ Worked Example

In △ABC, ∠A = 2∠B and ∠C = ∠B + 30°. Find all three angles.

Let ∠B = x. Then ∠A = 2x and ∠C = x+30°. By the angle-sum theorem,

2x + x + (x+30°) = 180°  ⇒  4x = 150°  ⇒  x = 37.5°.

So ∠B = 37.5°, ∠A = 75°, ∠C = 67.5°. (Check: they sum to 180°.)

☞ Worked Example

An isosceles triangle has its apex angle equal to 40°. Find the two base angles.

The two base angles are equal (Chapter 7); call each β. The three sum to 180°: 40° + 2β = 180°, so 2β = 140° and β = 70°. Each base angle is 70°. The angle-sum theorem plus one equality pins the whole triangle down. ■

➤ Your turn

The three angles of a triangle are in the ratio 3:4:5. Find all three, and classify the triangle by its angles.

Set-up (you finish it): the parts total 3+4+5 = 12, sharing 180°, so one part is 180°/12. Multiply by 3, 4, 5; then check whether the largest is below, at, or above 90°.

Answer: one part = 15°, so 45°, 60°, 75° — all below 90°, an acute triangle.

Three angles that looked utterly unalike are, in truth, one straight angle in disguise — and from that single fact a whole family of consequences unfolds.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Triangle: three non-collinear points joined in pairs; vertices, sides, interior angles.
  • Angle Sum: the three interior angles total 180° — proved by a parallel through one vertex.
  • Exterior Angle: equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
  • By angles: acute (all <90°), right (one =90°), obtuse (one >90°). By sides: scalene, isosceles (two equal), equilateral (all equal, each 60°).
  • Polygons: convex n-gon interior sum (n−2)·180°; exterior angles total 360°.

Chapter 5Congruence: When Are Two Things the Same?

✦ Wonder

A factory must stamp out thousands of identical metal triangles. To check a finished piece, an inspector is not allowed to lay it on top of the master copy. She may only measure it. What is the fewest measurements she needs to be certain the new triangle is a perfect copy — not merely close, but exactly the same?

The answer — remarkably — is three, and the story of which three is the theory of congruence. It is the first place geometry pays you a dividend: a short list of checks that guarantee two figures are identical, so you never have to slide one onto the other.

What congruence means

Definition · Congruent figures

Two figures are congruent if one can be moved onto the other — by sliding, turning, and if necessary flipping — so that they coincide exactly. For triangles this means all three pairs of corresponding sides are equal and all three pairs of corresponding angles are equal. We write △ABC ≅ △DEF.

The order of letters is a promise, not a decoration. Writing △ABC ≅ △DEF asserts six equalities at once: A↔D, B↔E, C↔F, so AB=DE, BC=EF, CA=FD and ∠A=∠D, ∠B=∠E, ∠C=∠F. Always list vertices in corresponding order.

The shortcuts: congruence criteria

Checking all six equalities would defeat the purpose. The great discovery is that the right three already force the other three.

Theorem · Congruence criteria

Two triangles are congruent if any one of the following holds:

SSS — three pairs of sides equal;  SAS — two pairs of sides and the included angle equal;  ASA — two pairs of angles and the included side equal;  AAS — two pairs of angles and a non-included side equal;  RHS — in right triangles, the hypotenuse and one other side equal.

The word included is the whole game in SAS and ASA. The angle in SAS must be the one squeezed between the two named sides; the side in ASA must be the one joining the two named angles.

Aha!

There is no “SSA” and no “AAA.” Two sides and a non-included angle need not fix a triangle, and three equal angles fix only the shape, not the size (that is similarity, the subject of Chapter 8). Knowing which letter-combinations fail is as important as knowing which succeed.

☞ Worked Example · The inspector’s three measurements

A finished triangle is checked by measuring one side, 6 cm long, together with the two angles at its ends, 50° and 60°. Is the triangle completely determined?

Yes. The measured side is included between the two measured angles, so this is exactly ASA — and ASA forces the whole triangle. (The third angle is pinned too: 180°−50°−60° = 70°.) This answers the Wonder: three well-chosen measurements — a side and its two end-angles — certify a perfect copy. ■

Why SSA can fail

It is worth seeing the failure, so the rule sticks. Fix an angle at A and a side AB. From B swing a segment of fixed length. If that length is right, it can reach the far ray at two different points C₁ and C₂ — giving two genuinely different triangles that share the same “side–side–angle.”

Congruence as a proof engine

The real power of congruence is indirect: to prove two segments or two angles are equal, find two triangles containing them, prove the triangles congruent, then read off the equality as “corresponding parts.” This last step is used so often it has an abbreviation: CPCTC — corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent.

☞ Worked Example

C is the midpoint of both AB and DE (the segments cross at C). Prove AD = BE.

Look at △ACD and △BCE. We have AC=BC (midpoint of AB) and DC=EC (midpoint of DE). The angles ∠ACD and ∠BCE are vertical angles, hence equal. That is two sides and the included angle: by SAS, △ACD ≅ △BCE. Therefore AD=BE by CPCTC. ■

✗ Common Trap

CPCTC may be used only after congruence is already established. Writing “AD=BE because the triangles look congruent” proves nothing. First earn the congruence with SSS/SAS/ASA/AAS/RHS; then harvest the corresponding parts.

☞ Worked Example

In △PQR, PQ=PR, and PS bisects ∠P with S on QR. Prove that QS=SR and that PS ⊥ QR.

Compare △PQS and △PRS: PQ=PR (given), ∠QPS=∠RPS (bisector), PS=PS (shared) — two sides and the included angle, so by SAS the triangles are congruent. CPCTC gives QS=SR (so S is the midpoint) and ∠PSQ=∠PSR; being a linear pair, each is 90°, so PS ⊥ QR. One congruence delivered both a length equality and a perpendicularity. ■

➤ Your turn

In quadrilateral ABCD the diagonal AC is drawn, with AB=AD and CB=CD. Which criterion proves △ABC ≅ △ADC, and what does it tell you about ∠B and ∠D?

Set-up (you finish it): the two triangles share side AC; with AB=AD and CB=CD that is three pairs of equal sides. Name the criterion, then read off the angles at B and D by CPCTC.

Answer: SSS, so △ABC ≅ △ADC and therefore ∠B = ∠D.

Congruence is the first real dividend geometry pays: three well-chosen measurements, and you know two figures are twins. From now on, whenever you must prove two things equal, you will hunt for the triangles that hold them.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Congruent (△ABC ≅ △DEF): identical after sliding/turning/flipping; letter order names the correspondence.
  • Criteria: SSS, SAS (included angle), ASA (included side), AAS, RHS (right triangles).
  • No SSA, no AAA: a non-included angle can give two triangles; equal angles fix shape, not size.
  • CPCTC: once triangles are proved congruent, all corresponding parts are equal.
  • Strategy: to prove two lengths or angles equal, find two triangles containing them and prove those congruent first.

↑ Contents

Chapter 6Compass and Straightedge

✦ Wonder

You are given only two tools: a straightedge (an unmarked ruler — it can draw a line through two points, but cannot measure) and a compass (it can draw a circle of any radius about any centre). No protractor, no numbers. With these alone, the Greeks built almost all of geometry. Can you, with just these two tools, cut any angle exactly in half — with no measuring at all?

You can, and you will, in this chapter. Constructions are not a quaint old game. They are proof made physical: every legal construction corresponds to a theorem about what must exist. And the discipline of using only these two idealised tools is what gives geometry its bedrock certainty.

The rules

Exactly two moves are permitted. Straightedge: given two existing points, draw the (infinite) line through them. Compass: given a centre point and a radius (the distance between two existing points), draw a circle. New points may be created only where drawn lines and circles cross. That is the whole game — and it is astonishingly powerful.

Construction 1: the perpendicular bisector

To construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment AB: open the compass wider than half of AB. Draw an arc centred at A, then an arc of the same radius centred at B. They meet at two points, P above and Q below. The line PQ is the perpendicular bisector.

Why it works. Both P and Q are equidistant from A and from B (equal compass radius). The set of all points equidistant from A and B is the perpendicular bisector — so P and Q both lie on it, and two points determine the line.

Construction 2: bisecting an angle

To bisect a given angle with vertex A: draw an arc centred at A, cutting the two sides at P and Q. Now draw two equal arcs centred at P and at Q; they meet at R. The ray AR bisects the angle.

Why it works. By construction AP=AQ (one arc) and PR=QR (equal arcs), and AR is shared. So △APR ≅ △AQR by SSS, and therefore ∠PAR = ∠QAR by CPCTC. Congruence, doing exactly the job it was built for.

Construction 3: the equilateral triangle (Euclid, Proposition I.1)

The very first proposition of Euclid’s Elements builds an equilateral triangle on a given segment AB. Draw a circle centred at A through B, and another centred at B through A. Where they meet is the apex C.

Why it works. CA=AB because both are radii of the first circle; CB=AB because both are radii of the second. Hence all three sides equal AB. It is hard to overstate how much rests on this little figure: it is, quite literally, theorem number one.

Building specific angles and lengths

The three basic moves combine into a surprising reach. Two short examples show the pattern — and answer the chapter’s Wonder.

☞ Worked Example

Construct a 45° angle with straightedge and compass alone.

First erect a right angle (the perpendicular construction); that gives 90°. Then bisect it by Construction 2. The perpendicular is exactly 90°, and bisection halves it: 90°/2 = 45°. No protractor ever touched the page — two certified moves, stacked. ■

☞ Worked Example

From a segment of length 1, construct a segment of length 2.

Construct a right angle at a point O, and with the compass mark length 1 along each arm, reaching A and B. Join A to B. By the Pythagorean theorem (Chapter 9), AB² = 1²+1² = 2, so AB = 2. An irrational length is built exactly, in three strokes; repeating the trick on the new hypotenuse builds 3, then 2, then 5, … — the spiral of Theodorus. ■

Aha!

Notice the rhythm of every construction: do, then prove. The compass and straightedge produce a figure; congruence (or the equidistance idea) certifies it is the figure we wanted. A construction without its justification is a magic trick; with it, it is mathematics.

Mathematician’s Margin

For over two thousand years, three construction puzzles resisted every attempt: trisecting an arbitrary angle, doubling the cube, and squaring the circle. Only in the 1800s, using algebra and the new idea of constructible numbers, were all three proven impossible with straightedge and compass alone. Some of the deepest theorems are about what cannot be done.

➤ Your turn

Outline how to construct a 30° angle with straightedge and compass.

Set-up (you finish it): you already get a 60° angle for free — it is a corner of the equilateral triangle of Construction 3. What single further move turns 60° into 30°?

Answer: build a 60° angle (a vertex of an equilateral triangle), then bisect it (Construction 2): 60°/2 = 30°.

Two tools, no numbers, and yet every figure you build arrives with a proof that it must be exactly what you claim. Construction is geometry rolling up its sleeves.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Two moves only: straightedge (line through two points) and compass (circle from a centre + radius); new points appear only where drawn lines/circles cross.
  • Core constructions: perpendicular bisector and midpoint; angle bisector; equilateral triangle (a 60° angle); perpendiculars; copying an angle; a parallel through a point.
  • Built angles: 60°, 30°, 15° (equilateral, then bisect); 90°, 45° (perpendicular, then bisect).
  • Every construction = do, then prove: the figure is certified by congruence (often SSS) or the equidistance idea.
  • Provably impossible: trisecting a general angle, doubling the cube, squaring the circle.

↑ Contents

Chapter 7Isosceles, Equilateral, and the Bridge of Asses

✦ Wonder

Fold a sheet of paper in half and cut a triangle whose base sits on the fold line. Unfold it: the two halves match perfectly. Some triangles have this hidden mirror; most do not. What does that single line of symmetry secretly force to be true about the triangle’s angles?

A triangle with two equal sides is called isosceles (from the Greek for “equal legs”). That one equality — two sides the same — ripples outward into a whole family of consequences, and gives us a theorem so central, and historically so feared by struggling students, that it earned a nickname: the Bridge of Asses.

The Isosceles Triangle Theorem

Theorem · Base angles

If two sides of a triangle are equal, then the angles opposite them are equal. That is, in △ABC with AB=AC, we have ∠B = ∠C.

Proof. Let D be the midpoint of BC and draw AD. Compare △ABD and △ACD: AB=AC (given), BD=DC (midpoint), and AD=AD (shared). By SSS, △ABD ≅ △ACD. Reading off corresponding parts: ∠B=∠C. As a bonus, ∠ADB=∠ADC; since they form a linear pair they are each 90°, so AD ⊥ BC — and ∠BAD=∠CAD, so AD bisects the apex too. ■

Aha!

One stroke — the line AD — did four jobs at once. In an isosceles triangle the median, the altitude, the angle bisector from the apex, and the perpendicular bisector of the base are all the same line: the axis of symmetry. Whenever you meet an isosceles triangle, look for this line. It is almost always the key.

The converse is also true, and just as useful for proving a triangle isosceles.

Theorem · Converse

If two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite them are equal. So ∠B=∠C implies AB=AC.

Proof. Drop the bisector of ∠A, meeting BC at D. Then ∠BAD=∠CAD, ∠B=∠C (given), and AD is shared, so △ABD ≅ △ACD by AAS. Hence AB=AC by CPCTC. ■

Mathematician’s Margin

This theorem is Pons Asinorum, the “Bridge of Asses” — Proposition I.5 of Euclid. The figure Euclid drew, with the triangle’s sides extended below the base, resembles a footbridge; and medieval students who could not “cross” it (master the proof) were teased as the asses who balked at the bridge. Take heart: with congruence in hand, you crossed it in three lines.

The equilateral triangle

An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal. Applying the base-angle theorem to each pair of equal sides forces all three angles equal — and three equal angles summing to 180° must each be 60°.

Corollary

A triangle is equilateral if and only if it is equiangular, in which case every angle is 60°.

☞ Worked Example

In △ABC, AB=AC and ∠A=40°. Find ∠B and ∠C.

The base angles are equal: ∠B=∠C. Since the three sum to 180°,  40° + 2∠B = 180°, so ∠B=∠C=70°.

☞ Worked Example · Using the converse

In △ABC, ∠A=50° and ∠B=65°. Show the triangle is isosceles, and name the equal sides.

The third angle is ∠C=180°−50°−65°=65°. So ∠B=∠C, and by the converse of the base-angle theorem the sides opposite them are equal: the side opposite ∠B is AC and opposite ∠C is AB, so AB=AC. Spotting two equal angles is the standard way to prove a triangle isosceles. ■

☞ Worked Example

In △ABC, AB=AC, and the exterior angle at B measures 110°. Find ∠A.

The exterior angle at B and the interior ∠B form a linear pair, so ∠B=180°−110°=70°. Since AB=AC, the base angles are equal: ∠C=70°. Then ∠A=180°−70°−70°=40°. ■

➤ Your turn

An isosceles triangle has an apex angle of 36°. Find its two (equal) base angles.

Set-up (you finish it): the base angles are equal; call each β. The three sum to 180°, so 36° + 2β = 180°. Solve for β.

Answer: β = (180°−36°)/2 = 72°. (These 72° base angles are exactly the ones hiding in a regular pentagon.)

One equality between two sides, and a single fold of symmetry hands you equal angles, a right angle, a bisector, and a median all at once. Few lines in geometry work as hard as the one down the middle of an isosceles triangle.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Isosceles: two equal sides. Base-angle theorem: AB=AC ⇒ ∠B=∠C; the converse proves a triangle isosceles from two equal angles.
  • Axis of symmetry: from the apex, the median, altitude, angle bisector, and perpendicular bisector of the base are one line.
  • Equilateral ⇔ equiangular, every angle 60°.
  • Strategy: isosceles → draw the axis of symmetry; two equal angles → suspect equal sides.

↑ Contents

Chapter 8Similarity and the Power of Ratio

✦ Wonder

On a sunny afternoon a metre stick casts a shadow 1.5 metres long. At the same moment, a tall tree casts a shadow 24 metres long. Without climbing, without any special instrument, you can state the tree’s height exactly. How can a shadow on the ground measure a height in the air?

The secret is similarity: figures that have the same shape but not necessarily the same size. Where congruence asks “are these identical?”, similarity asks the subtler and more powerful question “are these scaled copies?” — and the answer unlocks heights, distances, and a vast share of all olympiad geometry.

Same shape, any size

The intuition is everyday: a photograph and its enlargement show the same picture at different scales. Every angle is preserved, and every length is multiplied by one fixed number. Triangles are the place to pin this down precisely, because a triangle’s shape is completely controlled by its angles.

Definition · Similar triangles

Two triangles are similar, written △ABC ∼ △DEF, if their corresponding angles are equal and their corresponding sides are in proportion: ABDE = BCEF = CAFD = k. The common ratio k is the scale factor.

Three criteria — and the one you will use most

For congruence we needed three facts. Similarity is cheaper, because we no longer insist the sizes match — only the shape. There are three standard tests.

Theorem · Similarity criteria
  • AA — two angles of one equal two angles of the other.
  • SAS — an angle of one equals an angle of the other, and the two sides enclosing those angles are in proportion.
  • SSS — all three pairs of corresponding sides are in proportion.

Why two angles are enough. Fix two angles of a triangle; the third is forced by the 180° sum, so the triangle is determined up to size. Stretch it uniformly and the angles never change — you simply get a larger copy. That is exactly what AA captures: equal angles compel proportional sides. SAS and SSS are the back-ups for when you are handed sides rather than angles.

Where you will use it. AA is the workhorse of the whole book. Almost every time you “find equal angles” — from parallel lines, vertical angles, a shared angle, a cyclic quadrilateral (Part III) — a pair of similar triangles is waiting, and with it a proportion that cracks the problem. Train your eye to ask, at every figure: which two triangles here are similar?

☞ Worked Example

Solve the shadow problem: a 1 m stick casts 1.5 m; a tree casts 24 m.

The Sun’s rays strike both at the same angle, and both stick and tree stand vertically, so the two “object–shadow” right triangles share two equal angles: by AA they are similar. Corresponding sides are proportional:

tree heightstick height = tree shadowstick shadow  ⇒  h1 = 241.5.

So h = 16 m. The shadow on the ground measured the height in the air. ■

☞ Worked Example · An angle you are simply handed

In △ABC, a point D lies on AB and E on AC so that ∠ADE = ∠ACB. Given AD=3, AC=6, AB=8, find AE.

Compare △ADE and △ACB. They share the angle at A, and we are given ∠ADE=∠ACB; by AA they are similar. The subtlety is the correspondence: matching equal angles, A↔A, D↔C, E↔B, so

ADAC = AEAB  ⇒  36 = AE8  ⇒  AE = 4.

Notice we did not write AD/AB = AE/AC — that would pair the wrong vertices. Equal angles tell you which sides correspond; get that order right and the proportion is automatic. ■

✗ Common Trap

Similarity statements are ordered: △ABC ∼ △DEF means A↔D, B↔E, C↔F, and the proportion must pair sides accordingly. Writing the letters in the wrong order is the most common similarity mistake. And beware: just as SSA fails to prove congruence, “two sides proportional plus a non-included angle equal” does not prove similarity. The equal angle in SAS must sit between the two proportional sides.

Thales’ Basic Proportionality Theorem

The single most useful consequence of similarity appears the moment a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle: it slices the other two sides into matching proportions. Intuitively, a parallel cut makes a small triangle at the apex that is a scaled copy of the whole, so its sides keep the same ratios.

Theorem · Basic Proportionality (Thales)

A line parallel to one side of a triangle, meeting the other two sides, divides them in the same ratio. In △ABC with D on AB, E on AC and DE ∥ BC, ADDB = AEEC.

Proof (sketch). Because DE ∥ BC, the corresponding angles give ∠ADE=∠ABC and ∠AED=∠ACB; the angle at A is shared. By AA, △ADE ∼ △ABC, so AD/AB = AE/AC. A little algebra rearranges this to AD/DB = AE/EC. ■

☞ Worked Example · Whole side or part?

In △ABC, D lies on AB and E on AC with DE ∥ BC. Given AD=4, AB=10, and DE=6, find BC.

Since DE ∥ BC we have △ADE ∼ △ABC. Here DE corresponds to BC, and AD corresponds to the whole side AB — not to DB. Hence

ADAB = DEBC  ⇒  410 = 6BC  ⇒  BC = 15.

The trap is to divide by DB=6 instead of by AB=10: the side DE lives in the big triangle, so it must be compared with the big triangle’s full side. When in doubt, name the two similar triangles first, then read corresponding sides straight off the similarity statement. ■

The converse is equally prized: if a line divides two sides of a triangle proportionally, it is parallel to the third side — a clean test for parallelism. A special case is the Midsegment Theorem: the segment joining the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the third side and exactly half its length.

The geometric mean in a right triangle

Drop the altitude from the right angle of a right triangle to the hypotenuse, and similarity hands you one of the prettiest length relations in geometry — and a second route to Pythagoras.

☞ Worked Example

In right △ABC (right angle at C), the altitude from C meets the hypotenuse AB at H, with AH=4 and HB=9. Find the altitude CH.

In △ACH and △CBH: each has a right angle (at H), and ∠HAC=∠HCB (both are the complement of ∠ACH). By AA, △ACH ∼ △CBH. Matching the H-sides,

AHCH = CHHB  ⇒  CH² = AH·HB = 4·9 = 36  ⇒  CH = 6.

The altitude is the geometric mean of the two pieces it cuts: CH = AH·HB. The same pair of similar triangles gives CA²=AH·AB and CB²=HB·AB — and adding those two recovers CA²+CB²=AB², Pythagoras itself (we meet this head-on in Chapter 9). ■

➤ Your turn

A right triangle has its altitude to the hypotenuse equal to 6, and that altitude meets the hypotenuse so that one of the two pieces has length 4. Find the other piece and the full hypotenuse.

Set-up (you finish it): the altitude is the geometric mean of the two pieces, so 6² = 4·(other piece). Solve for the other piece, then add the two pieces for the hypotenuse.

Answer: other piece = 9, hypotenuse = 4 + 9 = 13.
Aha!

Similarity converts shape information (parallels, equal angles) into number information (equal ratios). That bridge — from geometry to algebra and back — is the single most productive idea in the whole subject. Almost every length you cannot see directly, you can reach through a proportion.

Mathematician’s Margin

A fact for later: if two triangles are similar with scale factor k, their areas are in the ratio k². Double every length and the area quadruples; triple the lengths and area grows nine-fold. Lengths scale by k, areas by k², and (in three dimensions) volumes by k³.

Congruence asked whether two figures are identical. Similarity asks the deeper question of whether they are scaled echoes, and that single shift lets a shadow on the ground weigh a tree in the air.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Similar △ABC ∼ △DEF: corresponding angles equal, corresponding sides in one ratio k (the scale factor).
  • Criteria: AA (two equal angles) — the workhorse; SAS (equal included angle + two sides proportional); SSS (all three sides proportional).
  • Basic Proportionality (Thales): DE ∥ BC ⇒ AD/DB = AE/EC; the converse tests parallelism. Midsegment: joins two midpoints, parallel to the third side and half its length.
  • Right-triangle altitude: CH = AH·HB, and each leg² = (its hypotenuse-segment) × (hypotenuse).
  • Scaling: lengths ×k, areas ×k², volumes ×k³.

↑ Contents

Chapter 9Pythagoras, Four Ways

✦ Wonder

Of all the theorems in mathematics, one is so important that over four hundred distinct proofs of it have been collected — by schoolchildren, by presidents, by Leonardo da Vinci. Why would anyone need four hundred proofs of a single fact? And what is it about a humble right triangle that has fascinated every civilisation that ever measured land?

We meet at last the most famous relationship in geometry. We will not be content to state it; we will prove it four different ways, because each proof reveals a different face of the same gem — and learning to see one truth from many directions is exactly the habit that makes a problem-solver.

Theorem · Pythagoras

In a right triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. If the legs are a, b and the hypotenuse is c, then a² + b² = c².

Proof 1 — by similar triangles

Drop the altitude from the right angle C to the hypotenuse, meeting it at H. This single line splits the triangle into two smaller ones, each similar to the original.

In △ACH and △ABC: both have a right angle and share ∠A, so by AA they are similar, giving AC/AB = AH/AC, hence AC² = AB·AH. Similarly △CBH ∼ △ABC gives BC² = AB·BH. Add:

AC² + BC² = AB(AH + BH) = AB·AB = AB².

With AC=b, BC=a, AB=c, this is a²+b²=c². ■

Proof 2 — by rearrangement

Take a square of side a+b and place four copies of the right triangle inside it, one along each edge. What is left in the middle is a tilted square of side c.

The big square’s area is (a+b)². It is also the four triangles plus the inner square: (a+b)² = 4·½ab + c². Expanding, a²+2ab+b² = 2ab + c², and cancelling 2ab leaves a²+b²=c². ■

Proof 3 — President Garfield’s trapezoid

In 1876, five years before he became U.S. President, James Garfield found a proof using half of that picture: a trapezoid built from two copies of the triangle and one right isosceles triangle.

The trapezoid has parallel sides a and b and height a+b, so its area is ½(a+b)². It is also three triangles: two copies of our right triangle (each ½ab) and the middle right-isosceles triangle (½c²). Thus ½(a+b)² = 2·½ab + ½c², which again gives a²+b²=c². ■

Proof 4 — Bhāskara’s dissection

The twelfth-century Indian mathematician Bhāskara gave a proof so vivid that, legend has it, he drew the figure, wrote a single word beneath it — “Behold!” — and considered the matter settled. Pack four copies of the right triangle into a square built on the hypotenuse c; they leave a small square hole of side b−a.

The large square has area c². It is equally the four triangles plus the small central square: c² = 4·½ab + (b−a)² = 2ab + (a² − 2ab + b²) = a²+b². ■

Aha!

Four proofs, one truth. Proof 1 leaned on similarity; Proofs 2–4 used area, three different ways. And these are a mere sample: over four hundred proofs are known. When you can prove a fact several ways, you do not just know it — you own it, and you carry several tools instead of one.

The converse, and a warning

Theorem · Converse

If a triangle’s sides satisfy a²+b²=c², then the angle opposite c is a right angle.

This is what made the Egyptian rope-stretchers’ 3–4–5 trick work: 3²+4² = 9+16 = 25 = 5², so the corner must be square. Whole-number solutions are called Pythagorean triples; (3,4,5), (5,12,13), and (8,15,17) are the famous small ones.

✗ Common Trap

Pythagoras holds only for right triangles. Before writing a²+b²=c², be sure there is a right angle, and that c is the hypotenuse (the side opposite it — always the longest). For a general triangle you need the Law of Cosines (Chapter 18), of which Pythagoras is the special right-angled case.

☞ Worked Example

A right triangle has legs 9 and 12. Find the hypotenuse, then confirm by the converse that (9,12,15) is a right triangle.

By Pythagoras, c² = 9²+12² = 81+144 = 225, so c = 15. Running it the other way: since 9²+12² = 15², the angle opposite the side 15 must be right. (Note (9,12,15) = 3×(3,4,5) — every multiple of a triple is again one.) ■

☞ Worked Example

Find the distance between the points (1,2) and (4,6).

Build the right triangle whose legs are the gaps Δx=3 and Δy=4; the straight-line distance is the hypotenuse:

d = (Δx)²+(Δy)² = 3²+4² = 25 = 5.

The distance formula of Chapter 21 is just Pythagoras wearing coordinates. ■

➤ Your turn

Is the triangle with sides 8, 15, 17 right-angled? If so, which side is the hypotenuse?

Set-up (you finish it): by the converse, the triangle is right exactly when the two smaller squares add to the largest. Check whether 8²+15² equals 17².

Answer: 8²+15² = 64+225 = 289 = 17², so yes — right-angled, hypotenuse 17.

Four hundred proofs and counting, for a single line of algebra about a corner. Some truths run so deep that every generation wants to discover them again in its own hand.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Pythagoras: right triangle ⇒ a²+b²=c², with c the hypotenuse (longest side). Right triangles only.
  • Converse: if a²+b²=c², the angle opposite c is right — the test for a right angle from side lengths.
  • Triples: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (7,24,25) and their multiples; the family (2mn, m²−n², m²+n²) generates them.
  • Distance = Pythagoras in coordinates: d = (Δx)²+(Δy)².
  • Classify (a≤b≤c): acute / right / obtuse as a²+b² is >, =, or < c².

↑ Contents

Chapter 10The Four Centres

✦ Wonder

Cut any triangle out of stiff card and try to balance it on the tip of a pencil. There is exactly one point where it balances perfectly. Now ask: where is the one point equally far from all three corners? And the one equally far from all three edges? Astonishingly, each question has a clean answer — and the points are, in general, all different. A single triangle secretly carries a whole constellation of special centres.

Every triangle hides four classical centres, each born from a different family of three lines that — against all odds — always meet at a single point. The fact that three lines pass through one point is called concurrency, and it is never an accident; each is a small miracle we can prove.

The centroid: where medians meet

A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. A triangle has three.

☞ Worked Example

Prove that two medians cut each other in the ratio 2:1 — and deduce all three medians concur.

Let E, F be the midpoints of AC, AB, and let medians BE and CF meet at G. By the Midsegment Theorem, EF ∥ BC and EF = ½BC. So △GEF ∼ △GBC (AA), with ratio EF:BC = 1:2. Hence BG/GE = CG/GF = 2: each median is cut 2:1 from the vertex. Since any two medians meet at the 2/3 point of each, the third must pass through that same point too — the three cannot help but concur. ■

Definition · Centroid

The three medians meet at the centroid G, which divides each median 2:1 from the vertex. It is the triangle’s centre of mass — the balance point of the Wonder.

The circumcentre and incentre

Two more centres come from equidistance, and each carries its own circle. A point on the perpendicular bisector of a side is equidistant from that side’s endpoints; where two perpendicular bisectors cross is equidistant from all three vertices — the circumcentre O, centre of the circle through A, B, C. The same argument with angle bisectors gives the incentre I, equidistant from the three sides — centre of the inscribed circle.

☞ Worked Example

Prove the strikingly simple formula ∠BIC = 90° + ½∠A.

Since I lies on the bisectors of ∠B and ∠C, we have ∠IBC = ½∠B and ∠ICB = ½∠C. In △BIC the angles sum to 180°: ∠BIC = 180° − ½(∠B+∠C). But ∠B+∠C = 180°−∠A, so ∠BIC = 180° − ½(180°−∠A) = 90° + ½∠A.

The angle at the incentre depends on ∠A alone — slide B and C however you like; as long as ∠A holds steady, ∠BIC never moves. ■

The orthocentre, and a vector miracle

The three altitudes (perpendiculars from each vertex to the opposite side) also concur, at the orthocentre H. The cleanest proof is pure magic with vectors — and it hands us a deeper theorem for free.

☞ Worked Example

Place the circumcentre O at the origin, so the position vectors a, b, c all have length R. Show the point H with position vector a+b+c is the orthocentre.

The direction from A to H is h−a = b+c; the side BC has direction c−b. Their dot product is

(b+c)·(c−b) = |c|² − |b|² = R² − R² = 0,

so AH ⊥ BC: H lies on the altitude from A. By identical reasoning it lies on all three altitudes — they concur at H = a+b+c. ■

That little computation does more than prove concurrency. The centroid is g = ⅓(a+b+c), so h = 3g. With O at the origin, the three centres have position vectors 0, ⅓h, h — three points on a single line through the origin, with OG:GH = 1:2.

Aha!

This line is the celebrated Euler line. In every triangle, the circumcentre, centroid, and orthocentre are collinear, with the centroid one-third of the way from O to H. Leonhard Euler discovered this in 1765, and it still feels like a conjuring trick: three centres defined in three completely different ways, yet they always line up. (The lone exception is the equilateral triangle, where all three coincide.)

☞ Worked Example

For the triangle A(0,0), B(8,0), C(0,6), find the centroid and the circumcentre.

The centroid is the average of the vertices: G = (8/3, 2). The right angle is at A (legs on the axes), so the circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse BC: O = (4, 3), with circumradius OB = ½BC = ½·10 = 5. Two centres read straight off the coordinates. ■

➤ Your turn

In a triangle, the incentre I satisfies ∠BIC = 120°. Find ∠A.

Set-up (you finish it): use the incentre formula ∠BIC = 90° + ½∠A. Set it equal to 120° and solve.

Answer: 120° = 90° + ½∠A ⇒ ∠A = 60°.

Four centres, each the “middle” of a triangle by its own rule, and three of them threaded forever onto a single line. A figure this familiar has no right to hide so much.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Centroid G (medians): divides each median 2:1 from the vertex; G = ⅓(A+B+C), the average of the vertices.
  • Circumcentre O (perpendicular bisectors): equidistant from the vertices; centre of the circumscribed circle. In a right triangle, the midpoint of the hypotenuse.
  • Incentre I (angle bisectors): equidistant from the sides; centre of the inscribed circle. ∠BIC = 90° + ½∠A.
  • Orthocentre H (altitudes): with O at the origin, →h = →a+→b+→c.
  • Euler line: O, G, H collinear with OG:GH = 1:2 (with nine-point centre N, 2:1:3); all coincide only for the equilateral.

↑ Contents

Chapter 11Area as a Tool

✦ Wonder

Area seems like the answer to a question — how much paint, how much carpet. But what if it could be a tool for proving things that mention no area at all? Suppose a point sits inside a triangle and you join it to the three corners. Three small triangles appear. Could simply comparing their areas prove a fact about lengths?

It can — and turning area from a measurement into a method is one of the most quietly powerful moves in geometry. We will write the area of triangle ABC as [ABC], and lean on one idea again and again: triangles that share a height have areas in the ratio of their bases.

One formula, many uses

Theorem · Area of a triangle

[ABC] = ½ × base × height. Any side may serve as the base, paired with the perpendicular height to the opposite vertex — all three choices give the same number.

That picture hides the key lever. If two triangles share the same height, their areas stand in the same ratio as their bases — because the ½ and the height simply cancel.

☞ Worked Example

A point D lies on side BC of △ABC. Prove that [ABD] : [ACD] = BD : DC.

Both small triangles have their apex at A, and their bases BD, DC lie on the same line BC. So both have the same height — the perpendicular distance from A to line BC. Calling that height h,

[ABD][ACD] = ½·BD·h½·DC·h = BDDC.

A ratio of areas has become a ratio of lengths. This single observation is the engine behind Ceva’s Theorem (Chapter 19). ■

Area from coordinates: the Shoelace Formula

Place a triangle on the coordinate plane and its area falls out of the vertices’ coordinates alone — no height to hunt for.

Theorem · Shoelace

For vertices (x1,y1), (x2,y2), (x3,y3), [ABC] = ½ |x1(y2−y3) + x2(y3−y1) + x3(y1−y2)|.

The name comes from how you compute it: write the coordinates in a column, repeat the first at the bottom, and multiply diagonally down-right and down-left — the criss-cross looks like lacing a shoe.

☞ Worked Example

Find the area of the triangle with vertices A(0,0), B(4,0), C(1,3).

Substituting into the formula,

[ABC] = ½ |0(0−3) + 4(3−0) + 1(0−0)| = ½ |12| = 6.

Check the easy way: base AB = 4 lies on the x-axis, and C is 3 units above it, so [ABC] = ½·4·3 = 6. The two agree. ■

Counting dots: Pick’s Theorem

Here is a small miracle for triangles — indeed any polygon — whose corners land on the points of a square grid. Its area can be found by counting, with no multiplication of lengths at all.

Theorem · Pick (1899)

For a polygon whose vertices are lattice points, with I grid points strictly inside and B grid points on the boundary, Area = I + B2 − 1.

☞ Worked Example

For the lattice triangle in Figure 11.2, there are I=3 interior points and B=12 boundary points. Find its area.

By Pick’s Theorem, Area = 3 + 12/2 − 1 = 3 + 6 − 1 = 8. No base, no height, no coordinates — just dots, counted. ■

Mathematician’s Margin

Pick’s Theorem feels like sorcery: how can the area of a shape depend only on how many grid points it swallows? The deep reason is that each interior point “owns” a full unit of area while boundary points are shared with the outside — the − 1 is a correction for the shape closing up on itself. It generalises to a profound link between counting and geometry in higher dimensions.

➤ Your turn

A lattice triangle has 6 grid points strictly inside it and 10 on its boundary. Find its area.

Set-up (you finish it): apply Pick’s theorem, Area = I + B/2 − 1, with I=6 and B=10.

Answer: Area = 6 + 10/2 − 1 = 6 + 5 − 1 = 10.

Area began as something to measure and ends as something to reason with — converting lengths into ratios, coordinates into answers, and grid dots into exact areas. A quantity you thought you understood turns out to be a key that opens other doors.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Triangle area = ½ × base × height, with any side as the base.
  • Same base, same height (apex on a parallel) ⇒ same area; a median halves the area, and the three medians cut the triangle into six equal pieces.
  • Shoelace: [T] = ½|x1(y2−y3) + x2(y3−y1) + x3(y1−y2)|; equals 0 exactly when the points are collinear.
  • Pick: lattice polygon area = I + B/2 − 1.
  • Area as a tool: shared-height area ratios become base ratios — the engine of cevian and concurrency problems.

↑ Contents

Chapter 12Chords, Arcs, and the Circle's Anatomy

✦ Wonder

Why are manhole covers round? Try a square lid: turn it diagonally and it falls straight through the hole. A round lid cannot fall in, no matter how you turn it. The reason is a single property the circle alone possesses so perfectly — every point of its rim is exactly the same distance from one central point. That one fact, pursued carefully, blossoms into the richest chapter of elementary geometry.

We now turn from straight lines to the curve. The circle is the set of all points at a fixed distance (the radius) from a fixed point (the centre). Everything else — chords, arcs, tangents, and the beautiful angle theorems to come — flows from that definition. First, the vocabulary.

The parts of a circle

The key terms: a chord joins two points on the circle; a diameter is a chord through the centre (the longest chord, twice the radius); an arc is a piece of the circle; a tangent line touches the circle at exactly one point; a secant cuts it at two. We record one fact about tangents now and prove its companions later: a tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact.

The centre, the chord, and the right angle

The single most useful fact about chords links them to the centre.

Theorem · Perpendicular from the centre

The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord. Conversely, the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it.

☞ Worked Example

Prove the theorem.

Let M be the foot of the perpendicular from O to chord AB. Compare right triangles OMA and OMB: OA=OB (both radii), OM=OM (shared), and both have a right angle at M. By RHS, △OMA ≅ △OMB, so AM=MB. The chord is bisected.

This hands you a right triangle whenever you see a chord — legs (half-chord) and (distance from centre), hypotenuse (radius). Pythagoras then ties the three together as r² = (half-chord)² + (distance from centre)². A chord problem is a Pythagoras problem in disguise. ■

☞ Worked Example

A chord of length 24 lies in a circle of radius 13. How far is it from the centre?

The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, giving a half-chord of 12. With radius 13 as hypotenuse,

d = 13² − 12² = 169 − 144 = 25 = 5.

The chord lies 5 units from the centre. (Notice the 5–12–13 triple quietly at work.) ■

☞ Worked Example · Reconstructing a broken plate

An archaeologist finds a curved shard. Across the broken rim she measures a straight chord of length 2a, and at its midpoint the rim bulges out a height s (the sagitta) beyond the chord. Show the whole plate’s radius was R = (a²+s²)/(2s).

Drop the perpendicular from the centre O to the chord; it passes through the chord’s midpoint M and continues to the nearest rim point N, so O, M, N are collinear, with MN=s and ON=R. Hence the centre is at distance OM = R−s from the chord. The half-chord a, the distance R−s, and the radius R form a right triangle:

a² + (R−s)² = R²  ⇒  a²+s² = 2Rs,

so R = a²+s²2s. From a chip of pottery no bigger than your palm, you recover the size of the entire original plate — the circle “remembers” its radius in any tiny arc. ■

Equal chords, equal tangents

Two quick companions, each proved by the same right-triangle idea.

Proposition

In a circle, equal chords are equidistant from the centre, and conversely. Also, the two tangent segments drawn to a circle from an external point are equal in length.

☞ Worked Example

Prove the two tangents from P are equal.

Join OT1, OT2 (radii to the contact points), and OP. Each radius meets its tangent at a right angle, so △OT1P and △OT2P are right-angled at T1, T2. They share hypotenuse OP, and OT1=OT2 (radii). By RHS the triangles are congruent, so PT1=PT2.

The contact points may sit at wildly different spots, yet the two “reach” distances are always identical — which is why a ball bearing seats symmetrically in a V-groove, and the secret engine behind the inscribed-circle tangent lengths of Chapter 10. ■

➤ Your turn

A chord of length 24 lies in a circle of radius 15. How far is the chord from the centre?

Set-up (you finish it): the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so the half-chord is 12; with radius 15 as the hypotenuse, the distance is 15² − 12².

Answer: 225 − 144 = 81 = 9.

The circle rests on a single idea — one point and one fixed distance — yet already it is paying out right triangles, equal reaches, and a radius remembered in a shard. We have barely scratched its rim.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Circle: all points at a fixed distance (radius) from the centre; a chord joins two points, a diameter is the longest chord (= 2r), a tangent touches once, a secant cuts twice.
  • Perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord — and gives the master right triangle r² = (half-chord)² + (distance from centre)².
  • Equal chords are equidistant from the centre, and conversely.
  • Tangent ⊥ radius at the point of contact; the two tangents from an external point are equal, with length OP² − r².
  • Three non-collinear points determine exactly one circle (centre = meeting of perpendicular bisectors).

↑ Contents

Chapter 13The Inscribed Angle Theorem

✦ Wonder

A striker runs straight down the wing toward the goal line. The goal is a fixed width, off to the side. As she runs, the goalmouth seems to “open up” and then “close” again — there is some best spot where the goal looks widest. Meanwhile a teammate notices something stranger: from every point along a certain curved path, the goal appears at exactly the same width. What is that magic curve, and why does the angle refuse to change along it?

The answer is one of the most beautiful and useful theorems in all of geometry — the Inscribed Angle Theorem. It connects an angle at the centre of a circle to an angle at its rim, and from that single link cascades a whole toolbox: right angles in semicircles, equal angles on equal arcs, and the secret life of cyclic quadrilaterals. This theorem, more than any other, is the engine of olympiad angle-chasing.

Central versus inscribed

Fix a chord AB. The angle it makes at the centre, ∠AOB, is the central angle. The angle it makes at a point P on the circle, ∠APB, is an inscribed angle. The theorem says one is always exactly twice the other.

Theorem · Inscribed Angle

The inscribed angle is half the central angle subtending the same arc: ∠APB = ½ ∠AOB.

☞ Worked Example

Prove the theorem (the case where O lies inside ∠APB).

Draw the diameter from P through O, reaching the circle again at D. This splits ∠APB into ∠APD and ∠DPB. Now OP=OA (radii), so △OAP is isosceles and ∠OAP=∠OPA. The exterior angle of this triangle at O equals the sum of the two equal base angles:

∠AOD = ∠OAP+∠OPA = 2 ∠APD.

The same argument on △OBP gives ∠DOB = 2 ∠DPB. Adding, ∠AOB = 2(∠APD+∠DPB) = 2 ∠APB, so ∠APB = ½∠AOB.

The centre O does not appear in the conclusion at all. Move P anywhere on the major arc and the central angle never changes — so the inscribed angle freezes, no matter where P stands. That is the striker’s magic curve: every point of the arc sees the chord AB at the identical angle. ■

Two corollaries that do half the work in geometry

Corollary · Same segment

All inscribed angles standing on the same chord, from the same side, are equal — each being half the one fixed central angle.

Corollary · Thales

An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.

☞ Worked Example

Why is the semicircle angle a right angle?

When AB is a diameter, the central angle ∠AOB is a straight angle, 180°. By the Inscribed Angle Theorem, the angle at P is half of that: ∠APB = ½·180° = 90°.

This gives a stunning test for right angles. A right angle is exactly an angle that fits inside a semicircle. So the set of all points from which a fixed segment AB looks like a right angle is precisely the circle with diameter AB. Carpenters use this in reverse: to check a corner is square, see whether it lies on the circle through the two ends. ■

☞ Worked Example

Chord AB subtends an inscribed angle of 40° at a point P on the major arc. A point Q sits on the same arc; a point R on the minor arc. Find ∠AQB and ∠ARB.

Q is on the same arc as P, so by “angles in the same segment,” ∠AQB=40°. For R on the opposite arc, AQBR is a cyclic quadrilateral, so ∠ARB = 180°−40° = 140°.

You were told an angle at one point and instantly knew it at every point of the circle — a single 40° measurement propagates around the entire rim. Information in circle geometry travels astonishingly far. ■

Cyclic quadrilaterals: a first look

Four points all lying on one circle are called concyclic, and the quadrilateral they form is cyclic. The inscribed angle theorem gives them a signature property.

Theorem · Opposite angles

If ABCD is cyclic, then ∠A+∠C = 180° and ∠B+∠D = 180°.

Proof. ∠A and ∠C are inscribed angles standing on the two arcs BD — one on each side. Together those two arcs make the whole circle, a central total of 360°, so the inscribed angles total half: ∠A+∠C = ½·360° = 180°. ■

Aha!

The converse is true too and enormously useful: if a quadrilateral’s opposite angles sum to 180°, its four vertices must lie on a circle. This is a favourite olympiad weapon — to prove four points concyclic, hunt for two opposite angles that add to a straight angle. We devote all of Chapter 14 to these cyclic quadrilaterals.

➤ Your turn

AB is a diameter of a circle, and C is a point on the circle with ∠CAB = 28°. Find ∠ABC.

Set-up (you finish it): since AB is a diameter, Thales gives ∠ACB = 90°; the three angles of △ABC sum to 180°.

Answer: ∠ABC = 180° − 90° − 28° = 62°.

One angle, measured at a single point, and the circle broadcasts it to every other point on the same arc. No theorem in geometry repays its keep more often than this one.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Inscribed Angle Theorem: an inscribed angle is half the central angle on the same arc, ∠APB = ½∠AOB.
  • Same segment: all inscribed angles on the same chord, from the same side, are equal.
  • Thales: an angle in a semicircle is 90°; conversely the right-angle vertices on a fixed segment AB trace the circle with diameter AB.
  • Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles sum to 180° — and the converse is the standard test for four concyclic points.
  • Equal arcs subtend equal inscribed angles; an angle bisector through the rim lands at an arc midpoint.

↑ Contents

Chapter 14Cyclic Quadrilaterals & Ptolemy

✦ Wonder

Drive four nails into a board at random and stretch a loop of string around them: you get a quadrilateral. Now ask — could a single circular hoop be slipped over all four nails at once, touching every one? For three nails the answer is always yes. For four, only sometimes. Hidden among those four positions is a single condition that quietly decides it.

Four points that lie on a common circle are concyclic, and they are the secret heroes of olympiad geometry. Spotting a hidden circle — four points you can prove concyclic — unlocks a flood of equal angles via the Inscribed Angle Theorem. This chapter gives you the tests to find those circles, and then Ptolemy’s theorem, a relation so powerful it contains the Pythagorean theorem as a single special case.

Tests for concyclicity

From the Inscribed Angle Theorem we already know two facts about a cyclic quadrilateral: its opposite angles are supplementary, and two vertices on the same side of a chord see it at equal angles. The converses are what make these into tools, and they are true.

Theorem · Concyclicity tests

Four points A, B, C, D lie on one circle if either (a) a pair of opposite angles of quadrilateral ABCD sum to 180°; or (b) C and D lie on the same side of line AB and ∠ACB = ∠ADB (equal angles on the same segment).

☞ Worked Example

In △ABC, the altitudes from B and C meet the opposite sides at E and F. Prove that B, C, E, F lie on one circle.

The altitude from B is perpendicular to AC, so ∠BEC = 90°. The altitude from C gives ∠BFC = 90° likewise. So E and F both see the segment BC at a right angle — and by the converse of Thales’ Theorem, every such point lies on the circle with diameter BC. Hence B, C, E, F are concyclic.

Two right angles standing on the same segment instantly summon a circle — the one with that segment as diameter. This single move appears in a startling fraction of olympiad solutions. ■

Ptolemy’s Theorem

Theorem · Ptolemy

For a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, the product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of opposite sides: AC·BD = AB·CD + AD·BC.

☞ Worked Example

Prove Ptolemy’s theorem.

The trick is one clever auxiliary point. On the diagonal AC choose K so that ∠ABK = ∠DBC.

First pair. Triangles ABK and DBC share ∠ABK=∠DBC (construction), and ∠BAK = ∠BDC (inscribed angles on arc BC). So △ABK ∼ △DBC, giving AKDC = ABDB, i.e. AK·DB = AB·DC.

Second pair. Adding ∠KBD to the equal angles shows ∠ABD = ∠KBC; and ∠ADB = ∠ACB (inscribed angles on arc AB). So △ABD ∼ △KBC, giving KCAD = BCBD, i.e. KC·DB = AD·BC.

Add them. Since AK+KC=AC, the two results combine to AC·BD = AB·CD + AD·BC. ■

Two dazzling consequences

☞ Worked Example · Ptolemy contains Pythagoras

Apply Ptolemy to a rectangle ABCD. All four vertices lie on one circle (each angle is 90°, so opposite angles sum to 180°). Its sides are AB=CD=a and BC=DA=b, and its diagonals are equal, AC=BD=d. Ptolemy says d·d = a·a + b·b, that is,

d² = a² + b².

That is the Pythagorean theorem, falling out of Ptolemy as the special case of a rectangle. A theorem we proved four ways in Chapter 9 is just one corner of this larger truth. ■

☞ Worked Example · Van Schooten

Let ABC be equilateral, inscribed in a circle, and let P lie on the arc BC not containing A. Prove PA = PB + PC.

In order around the circle the points are B, P, C, A, so BPCA is cyclic with diagonals BC and PA. Ptolemy gives BC·PA = BP·CA + PC·BA. Since the triangle is equilateral, AB=BC=CA; dividing through by that common side, PA = PB + PC. ■

Aha!

Notice the pattern of this chapter. A circle converts position facts (concyclic points) into angle facts (equal or supplementary angles), and Ptolemy converts them further into length facts (products of sides). Each theorem is a translator between the three languages of geometry — position, angle, and length — and fluency in all three is what problem-solving really is.

➤ Your turn

ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with AB·CD = 30 and AD·BC = 12. One diagonal is AC = 7. Find the other diagonal BD.

Set-up (you finish it): Ptolemy says AC·BD = AB·CD + AD·BC, so 7·BD = 30 + 12.

Answer: BD = 42 / 7 = 6.

Four nails hammered into a board at random, and out of them falls a relation that quietly swallows Pythagoras whole. The circle has been generous today.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Concyclicity tests: opposite angles sum to 180°, or two points see a segment at equal angles from the same side. Two right angles on a segment ⇒ all on the circle with that segment as diameter.
  • Ptolemy: for cyclic ABCD, AC·BD = AB·CD + AD·BC.
  • Ptolemy’s inequality: for any four points AC·BD ≤ AB·CD + AD·BC, with equality exactly when ABCD is cyclic in order.
  • Ptolemy ⊃ Pythagoras: on a rectangle it gives d² = a² + b²; on an equilateral triangle’s circumcircle it gives van Schooten’s PA = PB + PC.
  • Big picture: a circle translates position (concyclic) into angle (equal/supplementary) into length (Ptolemy).

↑ Contents

Chapter 15Power of a Point & the Radical Axis

✦ Wonder

Stand anywhere near a circle and draw any straight line through your spot; it cuts the circle at two points. Multiply the two distances from you to those points. Now swing the line to a new direction and do it again — a completely different pair of distances. Astonishingly, the product comes out exactly the same. Every line through your point carries the same secret product. What is this number that the point “remembers” about the circle?

That number is the power of the point, and it turns a whole family of length problems into one clean idea. It also leads to the radical axis, the hidden line of balance between two circles, and to one more surprising concurrency.

The power of a point

Theorem · Power of a Point

Let P be a point and a circle have centre O, radius r. For any line through P meeting the circle at X and Y, the product PX·PY is the same, with value |OP² − r²|. If P is inside, two chords give PA·PB = PC·PD; if outside, two secants give the same, and a tangent gives PT² = PA·PB.

Why OP²−r²? Take the one special line through P and the centre O. It meets the circle at distances OP−r and OP+r from P, so the product is (OP−r)(OP+r) = OP²−r². Every other line gives the same value — so this single quantity, the power pow(P) = OP²−r², captures it all. It is negative inside, zero on the circle, positive outside.

☞ Worked Example

Prove the interior case: two chords AB and CD meet at P inside the circle, then PA·PB = PC·PD.

Join AC and DB. In triangles PAC and PDB: the angles at P are vertical, so ∠APC=∠DPB; and ∠CAB = ∠CDB, both inscribed angles standing on the same arc CB. By AA, △PAC ∼ △PDB. Hence

PAPD = PCPB  ⇒  PA·PB = PC·PD.

The messy fact “every chord through P has the same product” is really just one pair of similar triangles, hiding behind the Inscribed Angle Theorem. Read for a point outside the circle, the same picture proves the secant case word-for-word. ■

☞ Worked Example

From an external point P, a secant meets the circle at A (near) and B (far), and a tangent touches at T. Show PT² = PA·PB; then if PA=4 and AB=5, find PT.

A tangent is the limiting case of a secant whose two intersection points have merged into the single point T; setting A=B=T in PA·PB gives PT·PT = PT². So PT² = PA·PB.

Here PB = PA+AB = 4+5 = 9, so PT² = 4·9 = 36 and PT = 6.

The tangent is the geometric mean of the two secant distances. This is exactly how you compute the distance to the horizon: the line of sight is a tangent to the Earth, so (your height)·(your height + diameter) is the square of how far you can see. ■

The radical axis

Two circles sit in the plane. Is there a point with the same power with respect to both? There are infinitely many — and they form a line.

Theorem · Radical axis

The set of points having equal power with respect to two non-concentric circles is a straight line, the radical axis, perpendicular to the line joining the centres. If the circles intersect, it is the line through their two intersection points.

☞ Worked Example

Prove that the three radical axes of three circles (taken in pairs) pass through one point — the radical centre.
