Let R be where the radical axis of ω1, ω2 meets that of ω2, ω3. At R we have pow1 = pow2 and pow2 = pow3, so by transitivity pow1 = pow3 as well. But that is exactly the condition for R to lie on the radical axis of ω1, ω3. So all three axes pass through R.

The proof is pure logic — transitivity of equality — with no computation at all. And it is useful: the radical centre is the one point from which the tangents to all three circles are equal. ■

Aha!

The power of a point quietly unifies three separate-looking facts (two chords, two secants, tangent-and-secant) into one number, OP²−r². Whenever a problem multiplies two distances along a line through a circle, think “power,” and the circle’s centre and radius are secretly in charge.

➤ Your turn

Two chords of a circle cross at an interior point P. The first is divided into segments of length 6 and 4; the second into a segment of length 3 and an unknown x. Find x.

Set-up (you finish it): equal products along the two chords give 6·4 = 3·x.

Answer: x = 24 / 3 = 8.

A single number, carried unseen by every point in the plane, and three separate-looking facts melt into one. The more geometry you learn, the fewer things there turn out to be.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Power of a point: pow(P) = OP² − r² — negative inside, zero on, positive outside.
  • Constant product: for any line through P meeting the circle at X,Y, the product PX·PY = |OP² − r²| is the same.
  • Tangent: PT² = PA·PB = OP² − r² — the tangent is the geometric mean of the secant distances.
  • Converse (concyclicity test): lines AB, CD meeting at P with PA·PB = PC·PD ⇒ A,B,C,D concyclic.
  • Radical axis: the equal-power locus of two circles, perpendicular to the line of centres (the common chord when they meet); three circles’ axes concur at the radical centre.

↑ Contents

Chapter 16Tangents & the Tangent–Chord Angle

✦ Wonder

A cyclist rounds a perfectly circular track. At the very instant she passes you, her direction of travel points along a line that grazes the circle — touching it at exactly her position and nowhere else. That line is a tangent. Now here is the riddle: the angle her path makes with the straight line back to any landmark on the track seems to “know” about the far side of the circle. A line that grazes the rim at a single point should be a stranger to everything beyond it. This one is not.

The tangent is the circle’s most subtle line — meeting it just once — and it hides two gems: a right angle that is always there, and the beautiful Alternate Segment Theorem, which links the tangent to inscribed angles clear across the circle.

The tangent is perpendicular to the radius

Theorem · Tangent–radius

A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact.

☞ Worked Example

Prove it.

Let the tangent touch at T, and let S be any other point on the tangent line. Since the tangent meets the circle only at T, the point S lies outside the circle, so OS > r = OT. Thus among all points of the tangent line, T is the one closest to O. But the closest point of a line to an external point is precisely the foot of the perpendicular from that point. Therefore OT ⊥ the tangent.

We proved a perpendicularity without ever measuring an angle — purely from “the tangent stays outside.” This single right angle is the seed of everything else about tangents. ■

The Alternate Segment Theorem

Here is the tangent’s most surprising gift.

Theorem · Alternate Segment

The angle between a tangent to a circle and a chord drawn from the point of contact equals the inscribed angle subtended by that chord in the alternate segment.

☞ Worked Example

Prove the Alternate Segment Theorem.

Let φ be the angle between the tangent at A and the chord AB. Draw the diameter AE from A. Because the tangent is perpendicular to the radius (hence to AE), the chord AB makes angle 90°−φ with AE; that is, ∠EAB = 90°−φ.

Now AE is a diameter, so by Thales’ Theorem ∠ABE = 90°. In △ABE the angles sum to 180°, so

∠AEB = 180° − 90° − (90°−φ) = φ.

But ∠AEB is the inscribed angle subtending AB from E, and E lies in the same (alternate) segment as C, so ∠ACB = ∠AEB = φ.

The tangent direction at A is an inscribed angle in disguise. So a tangent-chord angle can be used exactly like any inscribed angle in an angle chase — the bridge that lets a tangent “talk” to points on the far side of the circle, answering the Wonder. ■

Tangent lengths and the incircle

Recall that the two tangents to a circle from an external point are equal. Applied to a triangle’s incircle, this yields one of the most useful little formulas in all of geometry.

☞ Worked Example

Prove that the tangent length from vertex A to the incircle is s−a, where s = ½(a+b+c) is the semiperimeter and a, b, c are the sides opposite A, B, C.

Let the incircle touch BC, CA, AB at X, Y, Z. The two tangents from each vertex are equal, so set AY=AZ=x, BZ=BX=y, CX=CY=z. Reading the side lengths off the figure, a=y+z, b=z+x, c=x+y. Adding all three: a+b+c = 2(x+y+z), so x+y+z = s. Then

x = (x+y+z) − (y+z) = s − a,

and likewise y=s−b, z=s−c. Three messy tangent lengths collapse into the clean trio s−a, s−b, s−c — the engine behind the inradius r=Area/s, behind Heron’s formula, and behind a host of olympiad length-chases. ■

Aha!

Part III has been one long demonstration that the circle is a machine for converting between angles and lengths. Inscribed angles, cyclic quadrilaterals, Ptolemy, power of a point, the tangent–chord angle: each is a different gear in that machine. With Part III complete, you hold the entire circle toolkit — and you are ready for the techniques of Part IV, where these tools combine into the art of the angle chase.

➤ Your turn

A triangle has sides a=9, b=10, c=11. Find the tangent length from vertex A to the incircle.

Set-up (you finish it): the tangent length from A is s−a, where s = ½(a+b+c).

Answer: s = ½(9+10+11) = 15, so the tangent length is s−a = 15−9 = 6.

A line that touches the rim at a single point, yet speaks fluently about the far side of the circle. The tangent keeps its secret in plain sight: its direction is just an inscribed angle wearing a disguise.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Tangent ⊥ radius at the point of contact — the seed of every other tangent fact.
  • Two tangents from an external point are equal; the tangent length is OP² − r².
  • Alternate Segment Theorem: the tangent–chord angle equals the inscribed angle on that chord in the alternate segment — so a tangent behaves exactly like an inscribed angle in an angle chase.
  • Incircle tangent lengths from the vertices are s−a, s−b, s−c — the engine behind r = Area/s and Heron’s formula.
  • Pitot: a quadrilateral has an inscribed circle iff AB+CD = BC+DA.

↑ Contents

Chapter 17Angle Chasing, the Workhorse

✦ Wonder

You are handed a crowded diagram — circles, chords, a triangle, a tangent — and asked for one particular angle, buried deep in the tangle. There is no single formula for it. Yet a grandmaster glances at the figure and writes the answer in seconds. They are not guessing. They are chasing: stepping from one known angle to the next along a chain of tiny, certain deductions, until the unknown is cornered. How do you learn to see that chain?

Angle chasing is the most-used skill in all of olympiad geometry. It is not a theorem but a craft: combining the angle facts you already own into chains that march across a figure. This chapter assembles your toolkit, adds two powerful new results about circles, and then hands you the professional’s secret weapon — directed angles.

The angle-chaser’s toolkit

Everything you need is already proved. Keep this checklist in your mind’s eye; each item turns one known angle into another.

The toolkit
  1. Angles on a straight line sum to 180°; around a point, 360°.
  2. Vertical angles are equal.
  3. Across parallels: corresponding and alternate angles equal, co-interior supplementary.
  4. Triangle angles sum to 180°; the exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
  5. Isosceles triangle: equal sides face equal angles.
  6. Inscribed Angle Theorem; angles in the same segment are equal; angle in a semicircle is 90°.
  7. Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles supplementary (and its converse, to find circles).
  8. Tangent–chord (alternate segment) angle.

The art is choosing which tool, and where. Two habits help enormously: mark every pair of equal angles with the same symbol, and always ask “do four of these points lie on a circle?”

The angle between two chords

Two results synthesise the inscribed-angle theorem into exactly what a chaser needs.

Theorem · Chord angle, interior

If two chords meet inside a circle at P, the angle between them is half the sum of the two arcs it intercepts.

☞ Worked Example

Prove it, and apply it: arcs AB and CD measure 50° and 30°. Find ∠APB.

Draw the chord BC. Then ∠APB is the exterior angle at P of △BPC, so it equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: ∠APB = ∠PBC + ∠PCB. Now ∠PCB = ∠ACB, an inscribed angle on arc AB, so it is ½·arc AB; and ∠PBC = ∠DBC, inscribed on arc CD, equal to ½·arc CD. Hence

∠APB = ½(arc AB + arc CD) = ½(50°+30°) = 40°.

The inscribed-angle theorem and the exterior-angle theorem combine into “half the sum of two arcs” — the intersection point “averages” the arcs facing it. ■

Theorem · Chord angle, exterior

If two secants meet outside a circle at P, the angle between them is half the difference of the two intercepted arcs.

☞ Worked Example

Prove the exterior case.

Let the secants be P–A–B and P–C–D (with A, C the near points). Draw chord BC. In △PBC, extending PC to D makes ∠BCD an exterior angle: ∠BCD = ∠P + ∠PBC, so ∠P = ∠BCD − ∠PBC. Here ∠PBC = ½·arc AC and ∠BCD = ½·arc BD, therefore

∠P = ½(arc BD − arc AC).

Inside the circle you add the arcs; outside you subtract. Slide P from inside to outside and the rule smoothly switches sum → difference — and when P sits on the circle, it collapses to the plain inscribed-angle theorem. One idea, three faces. ■

Directed angles: the professional’s shortcut

A frustration of angle chasing is configuration dependence: the same theorem needs “θ” in one picture and “180°−θ” in another, depending on which side a point falls. Directed angles sweep this away. Write ∠(ℓ,m) for the angle of rotation from line ℓ to line m, measured modulo 180°. Then ∠(ℓ,m) = −∠(m,ℓ), angles simply add, and four points A, B, C, D are concyclic or collinear exactly when ∠(CA,CB) = ∠(DA,DB).

☞ Worked Example

Why directed angles are worth the trouble.

The ordinary statement “angles in the same segment are equal” needs a caveat: if C and D are on opposite arcs, the angles are supplementary, not equal — two cases, two diagrams. In directed angles both cases are the single identity ∠(CA,CB) = ∠(DA,DB) (mod 180°), because working modulo 180° identifies θ with θ−180°. So a directed-angle chase, once set up, is valid for every configuration at once — you prove “it holds in all cases” for free. ■

✗ Common Trap

Directed angles are measured modulo 180°, never 360°: a line has no “arrow.” So ∠(ℓ,m) = 80° and ∠(ℓ,m) = −100° mean the same thing. Never feed a directed-angle result into a formula (like the Law of Sines) that needs the actual angle — convert back to an ordinary angle first, reading the final figure.

➤ Your turn

Two chords of a circle cross at an interior point P, intercepting arcs of 84° and 36°. Find the angle between the chords.

Set-up (you finish it): for chords meeting inside, the angle is half the sum of the intercepted arcs, ½(84°+36°).

Answer: ½(84°+36°) = ½(120°) = 60°.

Angle chasing is less a theorem than a way of walking a figure: one certain step after another, until the unknown has nowhere left to hide.

Key ideas & formulas
  • The toolkit: line/point sums, vertical angles, parallels, triangle sum and exterior angle, isosceles, the inscribed-angle family, cyclic quadrilaterals (and the converse, to find circles), tangent–chord angle.
  • Interior chord angle = ½(sum of intercepted arcs); exterior (two secants) = ½(difference). On the circle they collapse to the inscribed-angle theorem.
  • Directed angles ∠(ℓ,m), taken mod 180°, simply add: ∠(ℓ,m) + ∠(m,n) = ∠(ℓ,n).
  • One concyclicity test for all configurations: ∠(CA,CB) = ∠(DA,DB).
  • Two habits: mark equal angles with one symbol, and keep asking “do four of these points lie on a circle?”

↑ Contents

Chapter 18Trigonometry in Geometry

✦ Wonder

You want the height of a distant mountain you cannot climb, or the width of a river you cannot cross. You are allowed to walk along your own bank and to measure angles with a sighting instrument — nothing more. With two angle readings and one pacing-off of distance along your side, you can name the far dimension exactly. How do angles alone reach across the uncrossable?

Synthetic geometry chases angles; trigonometry turns angles into lengths and back, by way of the ratios sin, cos, tan. Three relations — the Law of Sines, the Law of Cosines, and the area formula — let you compute any triangle from partial data, and they connect a triangle to its circumscribed and inscribed circles in a startlingly tidy way.

Ratios in a right triangle

In a right triangle, fix one acute angle θ. The three side ratios depend on θ alone:

sin θ = opphyp,   cos θ = adjhyp,   tan θ = oppadj.

These ratios are the dictionary between an angle and the shape of its right triangle. The whole chapter extends them to any triangle.

The Law of Sines — and a hidden circle

Theorem · Law of Sines, extended

In any triangle with sides a, b, c opposite angles A, B, C, and circumradius R, asin A = bsin B = csin C = 2R.

☞ Worked Example

Prove the extended law, and see why the ratio is the circumdiameter.

Draw the diameter BB′ from B through the circumcentre O. Since BB′ is a diameter, ∠BCB′ = 90° (angle in a semicircle). And ∠BB′C = ∠BAC = A, because both are inscribed angles standing on the same chord BC. In the right triangle BCB′,

sin A = BCBB′ = a2R,   so   a = 2R sin A.

The same argument at the other vertices gives the full chain. The common ratio is not just “some constant” — it is the diameter of the circumscribed circle. A single number, read off any one side and its opposite angle, tells you the size of the circle through all three vertices. ■

The Law of Cosines

Theorem · Law of Cosines

In any triangle, c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C, where C is the angle opposite side c.

☞ Worked Example

A triangle has sides 5, 8, and 7. Find the angle opposite the side of length 7.

With c=7, a=5, b=8, the Law of Cosines gives

7² = 5²+8²−2·5·8 cos C ⇒ 49 = 89 − 80 cos C ⇒ cos C = 4080 = ½,

so C = 60°. Look at the formula when C=90°: cos 90°=0 and it becomes c²=a²+b² — Pythagoras exactly. The Law of Cosines is Pythagoras with a correction term −2ab cos C that measures how far the angle is from a right angle. ■

Area, and the bridge to both circles

Theorem · Area

A triangle with two sides a, b enclosing angle C has area [ABC] = ½ab sin C. Equivalently, [ABC] = abc4R = rs, where R is the circumradius, r the inradius, and s the semiperimeter.

☞ Worked Example

Derive [ABC] = abc/(4R) from the two facts you now have.

The area is ½ab sin C. By the extended Law of Sines, sin C = c/(2R). Substituting,

[ABC] = ½ab·c2R = abc4R.

Two ideas from this chapter snap together to reveal that a triangle’s area, its three sides, and its circumradius obey one clean law. Rearranged, R = abc/(4[ABC]) — the circumradius from sides and area alone. Pairing with [ABC]=rs links the incircle into the same web. ■

Aha!

Synthetic geometry and trigonometry are two languages for one subject. A hard angle chase sometimes melts in one line of the Law of Sines; a stubborn length yields to the Law of Cosines. The expert keeps both channels open and switches the instant one looks easier — that fluency is much of what Part IV is teaching you.

➤ Your turn

Two sides of a triangle, of length 5 and 3, enclose an angle of 120°. Find the third side.

Set-up (you finish it): the Law of Cosines gives c² = 5² + 3² − 2·5·3 cos 120°, and cos 120° = −½.

Answer: c² = 25 + 9 − 30(−½) = 34 + 15 = 49, so c = 7.

A sighting instrument and a single pace along the bank, and the far mountain can no longer hide its height. Angles, it turns out, are a currency you can spend for length.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Right-triangle ratios: sin, cos, tan — SOH–CAH–TOA.
  • Law of Sines (extended): a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C = 2R — the common ratio is the circumdiameter.
  • Law of Cosines: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C — Pythagoras plus a correction that vanishes at C = 90°.
  • Area: [ABC] = ½ab sin C = abc/(4R) = rs — one quantity tying together the sides, circumradius R, and inradius r.
  • Switch languages freely: a hard angle chase can melt in one line of the Law of Sines; a stubborn length yields to the Law of Cosines.

↑ Contents

Chapter 19Ceva, Menelaus, and Concurrency

✦ Wonder

The three medians of a triangle meet at one point. So do the three altitudes, and the three angle bisectors. Each time, three lines — with no obvious reason to cooperate — pass through a single point. Is this luck repeated three times, or is there one master rule that decides, for any three cevians, whether they will meet? And a mirror question: when do three points, one on each side, line up straight?

There is a master rule for each question. Ceva’s theorem settles concurrency of cevians; Menelaus’ theorem settles collinearity of points on the sides. They are twins — almost identical equations — and together they reduce a huge class of “do these meet / line up?” problems to a single multiplication.

Mathematician’s Margin

Giovanni Ceva published this criterion in Milan in 1678. Its mirror-twin is far older: Menelaus of Alexandria proved the collinearity version around the year 100, while setting down the geometry of spheres for astronomers. The two results sat sixteen centuries apart before anyone noticed they were a single idea seen from two sides.

Ceva’s Theorem

A cevian is a segment from a vertex to a point on the opposite side. Let cevians AD, BE, CF have feet D on BC, E on CA, F on AB.

Theorem · Ceva

The cevians AD, BE, CF are concurrent if and only if BDDC · CEEA · AFFB = 1.

☞ Worked Example

Prove the “concurrent ⇒ product = 1” direction using areas.

Suppose the cevians meet at P. Triangles with the same height are in the ratio of their bases, so the cevian from A gives BDDC = [ABD][ACD] = [PBD][PCD]. Two equal fractions subtract cleanly, so this also equals [ABP][ACP]. By the same reasoning at the other two vertices, multiply all three:

[ABP][ACP] · [BCP][BAP] · [CAP][CBP] = 1,

since every area appears once on top and once on the bottom. A statement about three lines meeting is settled purely by areas, with no angle or length computed. The converse follows: if the product is 1, the third cevian must pass through the intersection of the first two. ■

☞ Worked Example

One theorem, two classic concurrences: medians and angle bisectors.

Medians. Each foot is a midpoint, so each ratio is 1 and the product is 1·1·1 = 1. By Ceva, concurrent (the centroid).

Angle bisectors. The Angle Bisector Theorem gives BDDC = cb, and cyclically a/c and b/a. The product is cb·ac·ba = 1, so the bisectors concur (at the incentre). Two famous facts that each took real work in Part II now fall out of one criterion in a single line apiece. ■

Menelaus’ Theorem

Theorem · Menelaus

Let a straight line (a transversal) meet the lines BC, CA, AB at X, Y, Z. Then BXXC·CYYA·AZZB = 1 (unsigned). With signed ratios the product is −1 — the single sign that distinguishes collinearity from Ceva’s concurrency (+1).

☞ Worked Example

Prove Menelaus by dropping perpendiculars.

Drop perpendiculars from A, B, C to the transversal, of lengths p, q, r. Where the transversal crosses a side, similar right triangles appear: at X on line BC, BXXC = qr; likewise CYYA = rp and AZZB = pq. Multiplying, the product telescopes to qr·rp·pq = 1.

Ceva and Menelaus are the same cancellation wearing two hats; the only real difference is a sign, +1 for “meet at a point,” −1 for “lie on a line.” ■

Aha!

Keep the twins side by side. Same three fractions; product +1 means the cevians concur (Ceva), product −1 (signed) means the points are collinear (Menelaus). When a problem asks you to prove a concurrency or a collinearity, reach first for these.

➤ Your turn

In triangle ABC, cevians AD, BE, CF have BDDC = 2 and CEEA = 3. For the three to be concurrent, what must AFFB be?

Set-up (you finish it): Ceva requires the product of the three ratios to equal 1, so 2·3·AFFB = 1.

Answer: AFFB = 16.

Two theorems, one product of three fractions, divided only by a sign: concur at a point, or fall along a line. Geometry is fondest of the pairs that are secretly one thing.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Cevian: a segment from a vertex to the opposite side.
  • Ceva: cevians AD, BE, CF concur iff BDDC·CEEA·AFFB = 1.
  • Menelaus: points on the three side-lines are collinear iff the same product equals −1 (signed). One sign separates the twins.
  • Trig form of Ceva: concurrency iff the product of the three sine-ratios ∠BAD/∠DAC … equals 1.
  • Both telescope: areas (Ceva) and perpendicular distances (Menelaus). Reach for these on any concurrency/collinearity — medians, bisectors, altitudes, Gergonne, Nagel.

↑ Contents

Chapter 20Stewart, Apollonius, and Lengths

✦ Wonder

You know all three sides of a triangle. Now someone draws a line from a corner to a marked spot on the far side — a median, an angle bisector, any cevian at all — and asks: how long is it? You have no protractor and no coordinates, only the three side lengths and where the cevian lands. Is that enough to pin down its length exactly? It is, and one elegant formula does it every time.

Part IV so far has chased angles and used trigonometry; this chapter is about lengths — specifically the length of a cevian. Stewart’s theorem is the master formula, and from it the lengths of medians and angle bisectors drop out as special cases. The proof is a small miracle of cancellation.

Mathematician’s Margin

The relation is named for Matthew Stewart, a young Scottish mathematician who published it in 1746 — though the special case for medians was already known to Apollonius of Perga some nineteen centuries earlier. Old theorems rarely have a single owner; they have a lineage.

Stewart’s Theorem

Theorem · Stewart

Let D lie on side BC of △ABC, with BD=m, DC=n, and cevian AD=d. Writing a=BC=m+n, b=CA, c=AB, b²m + c²n = a(d² + mn).

A memorable way to say it: a man and his dad put a bomb in the sink — man + dad = bmb + cnc, that is, amn + ad² = b²m + c²n.

☞ Worked Example

Prove Stewart’s theorem.

Let ∠ADB = θ; then ∠ADC = 180°−θ, and cos ∠ADC = −cos θ. Apply the Law of Cosines in each sub-triangle:

c² = d² + m² − 2dm cos θ,   b² = d² + n² + 2dn cos θ.

Multiply the first by n and the second by m, then add — the cos θ terms are equal and opposite, so they vanish:

b²m + c²n = d²(m+n) + mn(m+n) = a(d²+mn).

The one unknown we could not control — the angle θ at D — cancels itself out, because the cevian makes supplementary angles on its two sides and their cosines are negatives. What is left is a pure relation among lengths. ■

Medians and angle bisectors for free

☞ Worked Example · Apollonius / median

Show the median from A to the midpoint of BC has length ma with ma² = (2b² + 2c² − a²)/4.

For a median, D is the midpoint, so m=n=a/2. Stewart gives b²·(a/2) + c²·(a/2) = a(ma² + a²/4). Divide by a:

ma² = 2b² + 2c² − a²4.

Summing over all three medians gives ma²+mb²+mc² = ¾(a²+b²+c²) — the medians “carry” exactly three-quarters of the triangle’s total squared side-length, whatever its shape. ■

☞ Worked Example · angle-bisector length

Show the bisector from A has length ta with ta² = bc − BD·DC.

By the Angle Bisector Theorem, BD/DC = c/b, so BD = ac/(b+c) and DC = ab/(b+c). Then b²·BD + c²·DC = abc. Stewart says this equals a(ta² + BD·DC), so

ta² = bc − BD·DC = bc 1 − (a/(b+c))².

The bisector length is the product bc of the two enclosing sides, docked by a single correction BD·DC. It is always less than bc — a bisector can never reach the length its two flanking sides would suggest. ■

☞ Worked Example

Compute the median to the longest side of the 13–14–15 triangle.

Take a=14 (the side receiving the median), b=13, c=15. Then

ma² = 2(13²) + 2(15²) − 14²4 = 338 + 450 − 1964 = 5924 = 148,

so ma = 148 = 237 ≈ 12.17. Three side lengths in, one exact cevian length out — with no diagram measured and no angle ever found. ■

Aha!

Stewart’s theorem is the length-counterpart of the area and angle tools: feed it the sides and the split point, and it returns the cevian. Medians, bisectors, and the segments cut by a cevian are all one substitution away. Whenever a problem hands you “a cevian of length…,” Stewart is your first move.

➤ Your turn

Find the length of the median to the side of length 8 in a triangle whose other two sides are both 5.

Set-up (you finish it): the median to side a is ma² = (2b² + 2c² − a²)/4, here with a=8, b=c=5.

Answer: ma² = (50 + 50 − 64)/4 = 36/4 = 9, so ma = 3.

Three side lengths and a landing point go in; an exact cevian comes out, measured without a protractor or a picture. The sides, it seems, were keeping the answer all along.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Stewart: b²m + c²n = a(d² + mn) for a cevian d splitting a into m, n (“man + dad = bmb + cnc”).
  • Median (Apollonius): ma² = (2b² + 2c² − a²)/4; and ma²+mb²+mc² = ¾(a²+b²+c²).
  • Angle bisector: ta² = bc − BD·DC = bc[1 − (a/(b+c))²] — always less than bc.
  • The mechanism: the foot makes supplementary angles on the two sides, so the cosine cancels — a cevian's length is fixed by the sides and split point alone.
  • Whenever a problem hands you “a cevian of length…,” Stewart is the first move.

↑ Contents

Chapter 21Coordinates: Geometry by Algebra

✦ Wonder

The story goes that René Descartes, lying ill in bed, watched a fly wander across the ceiling and realised he could pin down its position at every instant by just two numbers: its distance from each of two walls. In that moment geometry and algebra became one subject. If every point is a pair of numbers, then every line is an equation and every theorem is a calculation. What does geometry feel like when you can simply compute the answer?

Coordinates turn pictures into algebra. A clever choice of axes can reduce a theorem that resisted every synthetic trick to a few lines of routine computation — the technique fondly known as bashing. It is not always elegant, but it is reliable, and a strong solver keeps it ready as a fallback that never fails.

The coordinate toolkit

Place the plane on axes. For points P=(x1,y1) and Q=(x2,y2),

PQ = (x2−x1)² + (y2−y1)²,   midpoint = (x1+x22, y1+y22).

For lines, the slope between P and Q is m = (y2−y1)/(x2−x1); parallel lines share a slope, and perpendicular lines have slopes multiplying to −1. A circle of centre (h,k), radius r has equation (x−h)²+(y−k)² = r².

Aha!

The art of bashing is the choice of axes. You are free to place the origin and axes anywhere. Spend that freedom wisely: put a right angle at the origin, a key side along the x-axis, a centre of symmetry at the origin. A good placement fills your figure with zeros and turns pages of algebra into a few clean lines.

Bashing in action

☞ Worked Example

Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.

Place it as in the figure: A=(0,0), B=(a,0), and since ABCD is a parallelogram, D=(b,c) and C=(a+b,c). The midpoint of diagonal AC is (a+b2, c2), and the midpoint of diagonal BD is the very same point. So the diagonals share a midpoint: each bisects the other.

A synthetic proof needs congruent triangles and several steps; in coordinates the two midpoints are simply computed and seen to be identical. The clever placement did all the work. ■

☞ Worked Example

Show the three medians of a triangle are concurrent, and find the meeting point.

Let A=(x1,y1), B=(x2,y2), C=(x3,y3). The midpoint of BC is Ma; the point two-thirds of the way from A to Ma is

A + ⅔(Ma−A) = (x1+x2+x33, y1+y2+y33).

This expression is symmetric in the three vertices — it does not care which vertex we started from. So the same point lies two-thirds along every median: the medians meet at the centroid, which is simply the average of the three vertices. The hard-won concurrency of Chapter 10 becomes obvious the instant you notice the formula is symmetric. ■

☞ Worked Example · The Apollonius circle

A point P moves so that its distances to two fixed points are in a constant ratio PA:PB = k (with k≠1). Prove the locus is a circle.

Place A=(0,0) and B=(d,0), and let P=(x,y). The condition PA² = k² PB² reads x²+y² = k²((x−d)²+y²). Expanding and dividing by 1−k² (legal since k≠1) leaves

x² + y² + (linear in x) + const = 0,

which is exactly the equation of a circle. A purely metric condition — “twice as far from here as from there” — secretly traces a perfect circle, the Apollonius circle. (When k=1 the squared terms cancel and the locus degenerates to the perpendicular bisector.) ■

✗ Common Trap

Bashing can bury you in algebra if you place the axes carelessly. Before computing, invest in the setup: exploit every right angle, midpoint, and symmetry to seed zeros. And once you have an answer, sanity-check it against the picture — a sign slip in coordinates produces a confidently wrong number with no warning bell.

➤ Your turn

Find the distance between P=(1,2) and Q=(4,6), and the midpoint of PQ.

Set-up (you finish it): PQ = (4−1)² + (6−2)², and the midpoint is ((1+4)/2, (2+6)/2).

Answer: PQ = 9 + 16 = 5; midpoint = (5/2, 4).

Descartes’ fly gave us a world where every point is a pair of numbers and every theorem a computation you can simply grind out. Sometimes the bravest move in geometry is to stop being clever and start counting.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Distance (Δx)²+(Δy)²; midpoint the average of coordinates; section in ratio m:n by the weighted average.
  • Slopes: parallel lines share a slope; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.
  • Circle: (x−h)²+(y−k)² = r²; complete the square to read centre and radius.
  • Centroid = the average of the three vertices.
  • Bashing strategy: choose axes to seed zeros — right angle at the origin, a side on the x-axis, symmetry at the origin — then compute and sanity-check against the figure.

↑ Contents

Chapter 22Vectors & Complex Numbers

✦ Wonder

Coordinates pin a point with two numbers, but they break the symmetry of a problem — you must choose which way is “x.” Vectors keep the freedom of direction without the bookkeeping. And the plane has a second, almost magical, arithmetic: treat each point as a single complex number, and suddenly multiplication performs a rotation. A whole category of problems, the ones built on turning, is about to fall open in your hands.

This chapter offers two more algebraic engines. Vectors handle midpoints, centroids, and perpendicularity with effortless symmetry. Complex numbers turn the plane into a number system in which translation is addition and rotation is multiplication — the cleanest possible language for any problem about turning.

Vectors

Write →a, →b, →c for the position vectors of A, B, C from a chosen origin. Then the midpoint of AB is ½(→a+→b), and — with delightful symmetry — the centroid of △ABC is ⅓(→a+→b+→c).

The dot product →u·→v = |→u| |→v| cos θ measures both length (→u·→u = |→u|²) and angle: crucially, →u ⊥ →v exactly when →u·→v = 0.

☞ Worked Example

Prove that the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular.

Let two adjacent sides from one vertex be →u and →v. A rhombus has all sides equal, so |→u| = |→v|. Its diagonals are →u+→v and →v−→u. Their dot product is

(→u+→v)·(→v−→u) = |→v|² − |→u|² = 0.

A zero dot product means the diagonals are perpendicular. The whole proof is one line, and it lays bare why: a sum-times-difference is a difference of squares, which vanishes precisely because the sides are equal. ■

Complex numbers: the plane that multiplies

Identify the point (x,y) with the complex number z = x + iy. Then addition z → z+w is translation by w; multiplication by eiθ is rotation by θ about the origin (multiplying by i rotates 90° counter-clockwise); and rotation about a point p by angle θ is z → p + eiθ(z−p).

☞ Worked Example

Square ABCD is labelled counter-clockwise, and you know A and B as complex numbers. Find C.

The side BC is the side AB turned 90° counter-clockwise at B. As a vector, AB = b−a, and turning it left is multiplying by i, so C−B = i(b−a). Hence

C = b + i(b−a).

Constructing a perpendicular of equal length — the heart of “erect a square” — is just multiplying by i. Every rotation problem that would need careful trigonometry in coordinates becomes a single complex multiplication. ■

☞ Worked Example

Prove a triangle with vertices a, b, c (as complex numbers) is equilateral if and only if a²+b²+c² = ab+bc+ca.

Let ζ = e2πi/3, a primitive cube root of unity, so 1+ζ+ζ² = 0. A triangle is equilateral exactly when one vertex is carried to the next by a 120° rotation about the centroid — algebraically, when a+ζb+ζ²c = 0 (one orientation) or a+ζ²b+ζc = 0 (the other). Multiplying those two expressions and using 1+ζ+ζ²=0 to collapse the cross-terms,

(a+ζb+ζ²c)(a+ζ²b+ζc) = a²+b²+c² − ab−bc−ca.

The product is zero iff one factor is zero iff the triangle is equilateral. So “equilateral” — a statement about equal lengths and 60° angles — is a single symmetric polynomial equation in the vertices. ■

Aha!

Three algebraic languages now stand beside synthetic geometry: coordinates (best for distances and circles), vectors (best for midpoints, centroids, and perpendicularity), and complex numbers (best for anything involving rotation or equilateral/square configurations). Part of mastery is sensing, at a glance, which language will make a given problem dissolve.

➤ Your turn

Find the image of the complex number z = 4+i under a 90° counter-clockwise rotation about the point p = 1+i.

Set-up (you finish it): rotation about p by 90° is z → p + i(z−p), so the image is (1+i) + i((4+i)−(1+i)).

Answer: (1+i) + i(3) = (1+i) + 3i = 1 + 4i.

Three algebraic tongues now answer to you, and a rotation that once meant a page of trigonometry has shrunk to a single multiplication. Choosing the right language is already half of solving the problem.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Vectors: midpoint ½(→a+→b), centroid ⅓(→a+→b+→c); dot product gives length and angle, with →u ⊥ →v ⇔ dot = 0.
  • Complex numbers: a point is z = x+iy; addition is translation, multiplication by eiθ is rotation (by i, a 90° turn).
  • Rotation about p: z → p + eiθ(z−p).
  • Equilateral test: a²+b²+c² = ab+bc+ca (via the cube roots of unity).
  • Pick the language: coordinates for distances/circles, vectors for midpoints/perpendicularity, complex numbers for anything that turns.

↑ Contents

Chapter 23Transformations

✦ Wonder

A cattle-hand at point A must ride to the straight river, fill a bucket anywhere along the bank, then carry it to the barn at point B on the same side. Where should she meet the river so the total ride is as short as possible? Trying points one by one is hopeless. But a single reflection turns the bent path into a straight one — and a straight line is the shortest thing there is. How can moving the whole picture solve a problem the picture refused to give up?

A transformation moves the plane — sliding, turning, flipping, or scaling it. The deep idea of this chapter is that the right motion can make a hard problem easy, because it converts the configuration into one you already understand. Reflections straighten paths; rotations create equilateral triangles out of thin air; scalings explain why certain figures are automatically similar.

Isometries: motions that preserve distance

A motion that preserves all distances is an isometry. There are exactly four kinds in the plane: translation (slide), rotation (turn about a centre), reflection (flip across a line), and glide reflection. Each carries any figure to a congruent copy — which is why an isometry never changes what we are trying to prove, only how easy it is to see.

☞ Worked Example

Solve the Wonder: find the point P on the line minimising AP + PB, with A, B on the same side.

Reflect B across the line to its mirror image B′. For any point P on the line, PB = PB′ (the line is the perpendicular bisector of BB′), so AP + PB = AP + PB′. The right-hand side is smallest when A, P, B′ are collinear — a straight line. So the optimal P is exactly where segment AB′ crosses the line.

The reflection converts “minimise a bent path” into “a straight line is shortest,” with no calculus at all. The same trick proves the law of reflection in optics and solves billiard-ball bank shots. ■

Rotation conjures triangles

A rotation about a point preserves distances and turns the whole plane by a fixed angle. Rotating by 60° is special: it manufactures equilateral triangles, because a segment and its image meet at 60° and have equal length.

☞ Worked Example

A point P inside an equilateral triangle ABC has PA=3, PB=4, PC=5. Find the side length.

Rotate the figure by 60° about A, sending B to C; let P map to P′. Then AP′=AP=3 with ∠PAP′=60°, so △APP′ is equilateral and PP′=3; the rotation sends P→P′ and B→C, so P′C=PB=4; and PC=5 is unchanged. Triangle PP′C has sides 3, 4, 5 — a right angle at P′. So ∠AP′C = 60° + 90° = 150°, and the Law of Cosines in △AP′C (with AP′=3, P′C=4) gives

AC² = 3²+4²−2·3·4 cos 150° = 25 + 123,

so AC = 25 + 123 ≈ 6.77. The numbers 3, 4, 5 looked unrelated until a 60° rotation folded them into a single right triangle. ■

Homothety: scaling from a centre

A homothety with centre O and ratio k sends each point X to the point X′ on line OX with OX′ = k·OX. It is not an isometry — it changes size — but it preserves shape: every figure maps to a similar figure, and every line to a parallel line.

☞ Worked Example

Show the medial triangle (joining the midpoints of the sides) is similar to the original with ratio ½, and explain why it is “upside-down.”

Let G be the centroid. The homothety centred at G with ratio −½ sends each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side: G divides each median so the vertex (at ⅔ of the median) maps to the point at ⅓ on the other side of G — precisely the opposite midpoint. A homothety multiplies lengths by |k|=½ and preserves shape, so the medial triangle is similar with ratio ½; the negative sign means it is rotated 180° — pointing the opposite way.

The medial triangle isn’t accidentally half-size — it is the original, shrunk by ½ and flipped through the centroid. (This same map is the key to the nine-point circle in Part V.) ■

Aha!

The strategic question a transformation answers is: “what motion makes this configuration familiar?” Reflect to straighten a path or exploit a mirror symmetry; rotate by the angle hidden in the problem (60° for equilateral, 90° for squares); scale by homothety to turn one circle or triangle into another. The transformation does not change the truth — it changes your view until the truth is obvious.

➤ Your turn

Towns A and B stand 3 and 5 units above a straight road, with a horizontal separation of 8. Find the length of the shortest path from A to the road and on to B.

Set-up (you finish it): reflect B to B′ (5 units below the road); the shortest path equals AB′, with horizontal leg 8 and vertical leg 3+5.

Answer: AB′ = 8² + 8² = 128 = 82 ≈ 11.31.

Slide it, turn it, flip it, shrink it: the figure never changes what it is, only how willing it becomes to confess.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Four isometries: translation, rotation, reflection, glide reflection — each preserves distance, so it changes only your view, not the truth.
  • Reflection straightens paths (Heron's shortest path, optics, billiards): a bent path becomes a straight segment to the mirror image.
  • Rotation conjures figures: a 60° turn makes equilateral triangles; a 90° turn, squares.
  • Homothety (centre O, ratio k): scales lengths by |k|, sends lines to parallels and figures to similar ones.
  • Composing reflections: two parallel mirrors give a translation (twice their gap); two intersecting mirrors give a rotation (twice their angle).

↑ Contents

Chapter 24The Configurations You Must Know

✦ Wonder

Take any triangle and mark nine special points: the three midpoints of the sides, the three feet of the altitudes, and the three midpoints joining each vertex to the orthocentre. Nine points, defined in three completely different ways, scattered around the figure. Now draw the circle through any three of them — and watch, astonished, as it passes through all nine. Why should a triangle be so generous?

From here on, the elementary tools rarely work alone; they combine into configurations — recurring constellations of points and circles that appear in problem after problem. Knowing them on sight is half the battle. We begin with the most famous of all: the nine-point circle, and the Euler line it completes.

The nine-point circle

Theorem · Nine-Point Circle

In any triangle these nine points lie on one circle: the midpoints of the three sides, the feet of the three altitudes, and the midpoints of the segments from each vertex to the orthocentre H. Its centre N is the midpoint of OH (O the circumcentre), and its radius is ½R.

☞ Worked Example

Prove the nine points are concyclic, with centre N and radius ½R.

Consider the homothety centred at the orthocentre H with ratio ½. It sends each vertex X to the midpoint of HX — exactly the three Euler points. So it maps the circumcircle (centre O, radius R) to a circle through those three points, with centre the midpoint of HO — call it N — and radius ½R.

The side-midpoints and altitude-feet are also images, under this same halving toward H, of points on the circumcircle (the reflections of H over the sides and over the side-midpoints all lie on the circumcircle). So all nine lie on the circle of centre N, radius ½R. The nine-point circle is simply the circumcircle shrunk by half toward the orthocentre — one homothety explains nine coincidences at once. ■

The Euler line, completed

We met the Euler line in Chapter 10: the circumcentre O, centroid G, and orthocentre H are collinear with OG:GH = 1:2. The nine-point centre now joins them.

☞ Worked Example

Locate N on the Euler line and give the ratios OG:GN:NH.

Put O at the origin. From Chapter 10, →H = →a+→b+→c and →G = ⅓→H; the nine-point centre is the midpoint of OH, so →N = ½→H. The four points have position vectors 0, ⅓→H, ½→H, →H — all multiples of →H, hence collinear. Reading the coefficients,

OG : GN : NH = ⅓ : ⅙ : ½ = 2 : 1 : 3.

A fourth centre, defined by a circle through nine points, lands exactly on the same line as the other three, at a clean rational position between G and H. ■

☞ Worked Example · A concrete triangle

For the 13–14–15 triangle, find R, the nine-point radius, and the inradius r, and check Euler’s inequality.

Here s=½(13+14+15)=21, and Heron gives the area K = 21·8·7·6 = 7056 = 84. Hence

r = Ks = 8421 = 4,   R = abc4K = 2730336 = 658,

and the nine-point radius is ½R = 65/16. Since R = 65/8 = 8.125 ≥ 8 = 2r, Euler’s inequality R ≥ 2r holds, with a little room to spare. ■

The incircle–excircle web

The incircle touches the sides at the contact triangle, with tangent lengths s−a, s−b, s−c (Chapter 16). Erected outside each vertex are the three excircles, each tangent to one side and to the extensions of the other two. These four circles weave a web of equal-tangent relations.

☞ Worked Example

The incircle touches BC at X; the excircle opposite A touches BC at X′. Prove X and X′ are reflections in the midpoint of BC.

From the incircle’s equal tangents, BX = s−b; the analogous computation for the A-excircle gives BX′ = s−c. Then BX + BX′ = (s−b)+(s−c) = 2s−b−c = a = BC, so X and X′ sit at swapped distances from the two ends — reflections in the midpoint M. A hidden symmetry links the circle nestled inside the triangle and the one bulging outside; it is the seed of the Gergonne and Nagel points. ■

Aha!

Olympiad problems rarely announce which configuration is hidden inside them. Training your eye to recognise “that’s a nine-point circle” or “those are incircle tangent lengths” is exactly what separates a solver who flounders from one who, like the grandmaster of Chapter 17, simply sees the structure and writes down the key step.

➤ Your turn

A triangle has circumradius R = 12 and inradius r = 5. Find its nine-point radius, and check Euler’s inequality R ≥ 2r.

Set-up (you finish it): the nine-point radius is ½R, and Euler’s inequality compares R with 2r.

Answer: nine-point radius = ½(12) = 6; and R = 12 ≥ 2r = 10, so the inequality holds.

Nine points that had no reason to agree, caught on a single circle; four centres strung along a single line. In this country the coincidences are never coincidences.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Nine-point circle: 3 side-midpoints, 3 altitude-feet, 3 Euler points lie on one circle, centre N = midpoint of OH, radius ½R — the circumcircle halved toward H.
  • Euler line: O, G, N, H collinear with OG:GN:NH = 2:1:3.
  • Contact lengths: the incircle touches the sides at distances s−a, s−b, s−c from the vertices.
  • In/ex symmetry: incircle and A-excircle touch BC at points symmetric about its midpoint, a distance |b−c| apart.
  • Feuerbach: the nine-point circle is tangent to the incircle and all three excircles. Learn to recognise these configurations on sight.

Chapter 25Concurrency & Collinearity, Top Level

✦ Wonder

Three circles are sprinkled on the page, overlapping every which way. Each pair shares a “line of balance” — the radical axis along which a point has equal power to both. Draw all three of these lines and they slam through a single point, every time. And there is a dual marvel: every point in the plane secretly names a line, and every line a point, in a way that turns theorems about meeting into theorems about lying on. Behind both marvels hums a single piece of machinery.

At the top level, proving that lines meet or points line up calls for heavier machinery: the radical centre, the duality of poles and polars, and the projective invariance of the cross-ratio. These turn whole families of olympiad problems into near-mechanical checks.

The radical centre

Theorem · Radical Centre

Given three circles with non-collinear centres, the three pairwise radical axes are concurrent. Their common point — the radical centre — has equal power with respect to all three circles.

☞ Worked Example

Prove the concurrency, and say what the radical centre is good for.

Let R be where the radical axis of ω1, ω2 meets that of ω2, ω3. There pow1 = pow2 and pow2 = pow3, so pow1 = pow3 — meaning R lies on the third radical axis too. All three concur. Because R has equal power to all three circles, the tangent lengths from R are equal, so R is the centre of the unique circle cutting all three orthogonally.

The proof is one line of transitivity — no computation. To prove three lines concurrent, it often suffices to recognise them as three radical axes; the conspiracy is then automatic. ■

Poles and polars

Fix a circle of centre O, radius r. To each point P≠O we attach a line, its polar: the line perpendicular to OP at the inverse point P* (with OP·OP* = r²). Conversely each line has a pole.

☞ Worked Example

Show the polar of an external point is its chord of contact, and prove La Hire’s theorem: P lies on the polar of Q if and only if Q lies on the polar of P.

From P outside, draw the two tangents, touching at T1, T2. Each contact point has OTi ⊥ PTi, and the line T1T2 is perpendicular to OP at P* — exactly the polar of P.

For La Hire, the polar of P is the set of points X with →OP·→OX = r². This relation is symmetric in P and X: “Q on the polar of P” is the very same equation as “P on the polar of Q.” This is a genuine duality — prove a collinearity, and you have proved a concurrency for free. ■

The cross-ratio and harmonic division

Projective geometry’s master invariant is the cross-ratio of four collinear points,

(A,B;C,D) = ACCB ⁄ ADDB,

which is unchanged by projection from one line to another. When it equals −1 (signed), the points are a harmonic range: then C and D divide AB internally and externally in the same ratio.

☞ Worked Example

Why the cross-ratio matters: state its power in one principle.

Projection preserves the cross-ratio. If four collinear points are projected from a centre onto another line, the four images have the same cross-ratio. So any property defined purely by a cross-ratio — above all, being harmonic (−1) — survives projection, and can be transported from a convenient figure to the target one. (A fundamental instance: P, its polar, and any secant through P always produce a harmonic range, linking this section to the last.)

Lengths and angles are mangled by projection, but one combination of four lengths is sacred — which is why a problem can be projected into a simpler picture, solved there, and projected back. ■

Aha!

Three master tools for the hardest concurrency/collinearity problems: radical axes (when circles are present, look for equal powers), poles and polars (to dualise incidences and exploit symmetry), and the cross-ratio (to project a hard figure into an easy one). Each converts a fact you cannot see into an equation you can check.

➤ Your turn

Points A=0, B=8, C=2 lie on a number line. Find the point D for which (A,B;C,D) = −1 (the harmonic conjugate of C).

Set-up (you finish it): C divides AB internally in ratio AC:CB = 2:6 = 1:3; the harmonic conjugate D divides AB externally in the same ratio 1:3.

Answer: D = (1·8 − 3·0)/(1 − 3) = 8/(−2) = −4.

Radical axes, polars, cross-ratios: three machines for seeing the unseeable, each turning a stubborn picture into an equation you can simply check. The hardest problems are not harder than the rest, only better hidden.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Radical centre: three circles’ pairwise radical axes concur; the centre has equal power (equal tangents) to all three.
  • Polar of P: the line ⊥ OP through the inverse point (OP·OP* = r²); for an external point, the chord of contact of the two tangents.
  • La Hire (duality): P on the polar of Q ⇔ Q on the polar of P — a collinearity gives a concurrency for free.
  • Cross-ratio (A,B;C,D) is preserved by projection; = −1 is a harmonic range.
  • Strategy: circles → radical axes; incidences → poles/polars; awkward figure → project via the cross-ratio.

↑ Contents

Chapter 26Spiral Similarity

✦ Wonder

A single transformation can both turn a figure and resize it about one fixed point — a “spiral similarity.” Here is the startling part: given any two segments in the plane, there is exactly one spiral similarity carrying the first onto the second, and its centre can be found as the meeting point of two cleverly chosen circles. Olympiad problems hide this centre everywhere. It waits, every time, at the crossing of two circles you will soon know how to summon.

A spiral similarity centred at O is a rotation about O composed with a homothety about the same O: it sends each point z to O + k eiθ(z−O). It scales by k and turns by θ, all about one centre — the secret engine behind a huge fraction of hard olympiad configurations.

One complex number says it all

☞ Worked Example

Show there is a unique spiral similarity sending A↦C and B↦D, and find its multiplier and centre.

A spiral similarity has the form f(z) = O + w(z−O) for a fixed complex w = k eiθ. Imposing f(A)=C and f(B)=D, subtract to get C−D = w(A−B), so

w = C−DA−B,   and then   O = C − wA1 − w.

Both w and O are determined (valid unless w=1, a pure translation), so the spiral similarity is unique. The entire rotation-and-scaling is captured by the single complex number w = (C−D)/(A−B) — its modulus is the scale factor, its argument the rotation angle. ■

The centre lives at a circle crossing

The complex formula is decisive but hides the geometry. The geometric truth is the lemma every olympiad solver memorises.

Theorem · Spiral Similarity Lemma

Let A, B, C, D be four points and let lines AB and CD meet at P. Then the centre of the spiral similarity sending A↦C and B↦D is the second intersection of the circumcircles of △PAC and △PBD.

☞ Worked Example

Prove the lemma.

Let O be the spiral centre taking A↦C, B↦D. Because O is fixed and the map scales and rotates equally, △OAC ∼ △OBD and △OAB ∼ △OCD. From the second, ∠OAB = ∠OCD; since P lies on lines AB and CD, this reads (in directed angles) ∠OAP = ∠OCP — exactly the condition that O, A, C, P are concyclic. So O lies on circle (PAC); the same argument puts O on circle (PBD). Hence O is their second common point.

To locate a spiral centre you compute nothing — you draw two circles and take their other intersection. This is the famous “Miquel point” move. ■

Aha!

The lemma has a twin reading: the same point O is the centre of the spiral similarity sending A↦B, C↦D (pairing the other way). One circle-crossing serves two maps. Whenever you see two segments whose endpoints could correspond, suspect a spiral similarity and hunt for its centre at a circle intersection — it converts ratios and angles between the two segments into one clean transformation.

➤ Your turn

Find the complex multiplier w of the spiral similarity sending the segment A=0, B=2 to the segment C=0, D=2i, and read off its scale factor and rotation angle.

Set-up (you finish it): w = (C−D)/(A−B) = (0−2i)/(0−2); then |w| is the scale and arg w the angle.

Answer: w = (−2i)/(−2) = i, so the scale is |i| = 1 and the rotation is 90° — a pure quarter-turn.

Two segments that looked unrelated turn out to be one turn-and-scale apart, their pivot hiding at a circle crossing. Once you have seen a spiral similarity, you begin to find it everywhere.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Spiral similarity: f(z) = O + k eiθ(z−O) — a rotation through θ and scaling by k, both about one centre.
  • One complex number: the map A↦C, B↦D has multiplier w = (C−D)/(A−B) and centre O = (C−wA)/(1−w) — hence unique.
  • Spiral Similarity Lemma: with P = AB∩CD, the centre is the second intersection of circumcircles (PAC) and (PBD) — the Miquel point.
  • Twin reading: the same centre also realises A↦B, C↦D.
  • Cue: two segments whose endpoints might correspond ⇒ suspect a spiral similarity, find its centre at a circle crossing.

↑ Contents

Chapter 27Inversion: The Great Simplifier

✦ Wonder

Imagine a transformation that turns the inside of a circle out and the outside in — sending points near the centre flying to infinity and distant points crowding toward the centre. Under this strange map, circles can become straight lines. A tangle of circles tangent to one another can be combed into a stack of parallel lines, where the problem is suddenly trivial. There is exactly one motion that does this, and turning it on the right point feels, every time, like a small act of magic.

Inversion is the most powerful single weapon in the olympiad arsenal. It is not an isometry — it badly distorts distances — but it tames circles, tangencies, and angles so beautifully that an impossible-looking circle problem can melt into a line problem. Used well, it feels like cheating.

What inversion does

Definition · Inversion

Fix a centre O and radius r. The inversion sends each point P≠O to the point P′ on ray OP with OP·OP′ = r². Points inside the circle of inversion go outside and vice versa; points on the circle stay put.

Theorem · Inversion’s behaviour

Under inversion with centre O:

  1. a line through O maps to itself;
  2. a line not through O maps to a circle through O (and vice versa);
  3. a circle not through O maps to a circle not through O;
  4. the angle between two curves is preserved (inversion is conformal); tangency is preserved.
☞ Worked Example

Why does a circle through O become a line?

Let the circle through O have OX as the diameter from O. For any other point P on it, ∠OPX = 90° (angle in a semicircle). Invert: P↦P′ and X↦X′ with OP·OP′ = OX·OX′ = r². From OP/OX = OX′/OP′ the triangles OPX and OX′P′ are similar, and the right angle at P transfers to X′. So every image P′ lies on the fixed line through X′ perpendicular to OX. That line is the image of the circle.

The inscribed right angle becomes a constant right angle at the fixed point X′, pinning every image to a single straight line. Inversion converts “angle in a semicircle” into “perpendicular to a fixed segment.” ■

Ptolemy, for free

Theorem · Distance under inversion

If inversion with centre O, radius r sends P↦P′ and Q↦Q′, then P′Q′ = PQ·r²OP·OQ.

☞ Worked Example · Ptolemy’s inequality

For any four points, AC·BD ≤ AB·CD + AD·BC, with equality iff ABCD is cyclic (in order).

Invert about A with radius r; let B, C, D map to B′, C′, D′. The distance law gives B′C′ = BC·r²/(AB·AC), and likewise for C′D′ and B′D′. The plain triangle inequality B′D′ ≤ B′C′ + C′D′, multiplied through by AB·AC·AD/r², becomes

BD·AC ≤ BC·AD + CD·AB.

That is Ptolemy’s inequality. Equality holds exactly when B′, C′, D′ are collinear — which, inverting back, is precisely when A, B, C, D lie on a circle. Ptolemy’s theorem, which cost a clever auxiliary point in Chapter 14, here falls out of the triangle inequality after one inversion. ■

Inverting to kill a tangency

Aha!

The strategic move: invert centred at a point where many circles or lines pass, especially a point of tangency. Two circles tangent at O both become lines (each is a circle through O), and tangent at O means the lines are parallel. A forest of mutually tangent circles can become a simple ladder of parallel lines, where lengths and ratios are obvious — then invert back. Choosing the centre wisely is the whole art.

This is how problems about chains of tangent circles — Steiner chains, the arbelos, Descartes’ circle theorem — are routinely dismantled: invert at a tangency, solve the easy parallel-line picture, return.

➤ Your turn

An inversion has centre O and radius r=6. Two points satisfy OP=3, OQ=4, and PQ=2. Find the distance P′Q′ between their images.

Set-up (you finish it): the distance law gives P′Q′ = PQ·r²/(OP·OQ) = 2·36/(3·4).

Answer: P′Q′ = 2·36/12 = 2·3 = 6.

Inversion asks you to turn the plane inside out and trust that the mess will fall into order on the far side. Master it, and the circles that once frightened you become the easiest things in the room.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Inversion (centre O, radius r): P↦P′ on ray OP with OP·OP′ = r²; inside ↔ outside, the circle of inversion fixed.
  • Behaviour: a line through O → itself; a line not through O ↔ a circle through O; a circle not through O → a circle; angles and tangency preserved (conformal).
  • Distance law: P′Q′ = PQ·r²/(OP·OQ).
  • Ptolemy for free: inverting at A turns Ptolemy’s inequality into the triangle inequality on the images (equality ⇔ images collinear ⇔ concyclic).
  • The strategic move: invert at a point of tangency — two tangent circles become parallel lines, where ratios are obvious; solve there, then invert back.

↑ Contents

Chapter 28The Computational Arts

✦ Wonder

Some olympiad problems are so laden with special points — centroid, incentre, orthocentre, contact points — that synthetic cleverness drowns. For these, the masters reach for a coordinate system custom-built for triangles, in which the centroid is simply (1:1:1) and the incentre is (a:b:c). In this system the triangle’s own structure does the bookkeeping. What would coordinates look like if a triangle, not a pair of axes, were the frame of reference?

Part IV gave you trigonometric, coordinate, vector, and complex “bashing.” This chapter adds the most triangle-friendly engine of all — barycentric coordinates — and then steps back to ask the strategic question: with five computational weapons available, which should you draw?

Barycentric coordinates

Fix a reference triangle ABC. Any point P can be written as a weighted average of the vertices, P = αA + βB + γC with α+β+γ = 1, and the triple (α:β:γ) is the barycentric coordinates of P. Geometrically α, β, γ are proportional to the areas of the sub-triangles PBC, PCA, PAB — which is why these are also called areal coordinates.

Mathematician’s Margin

Barycentric coordinates were the invention of August Möbius, who introduced them in 1827 by imagining weights hung at the triangle’s corners and asking where the whole would balance. The same Möbius later described the one-sided strip that still bears his name.

The reward is a dictionary in which the triangle’s centres become memorable triples: the centroid is (1:1:1), the incentre (a:b:c), the circumcentre (a²(b²+c²−a²):···), and the orthocentre (tan A:tan B:tan C).

☞ Worked Example

Prove the incentre has barycentric coordinates (a:b:c).

The incentre I lies on the bisector from A, which meets BC at D with BD:DC = c:b (Angle Bisector Theorem). In barycentrics, D = (0:b:c), so the bisector from A is the line of points (t:b:c). By the symmetric argument the bisector from B is (a:t:c). The common point makes the ratios consistent across both, giving I = (a:b:c).

The incentre — defined by equal distances to the sides — has coordinates that are simply the side lengths. Every classical centre collapses to a clean triple, and a problem about “the incentre and the centroid and the orthocentre” becomes algebra among (a:b:c), (1:1:1), (tan A:tan B:tan C). ■

☞ Worked Example

Show that three cevians from the vertices are concurrent precisely when Ceva’s product is 1 — recovering Ceva almost for free.

A cevian from A hits BC at (0:m:n), so it is the line through A=(1:0:0) and (0:m:n). Three such cevians are concurrent exactly when a 3×3 determinant vanishes — and expanding it gives precisely BDDC·CEEA·AFFB = 1.

Ceva’s theorem, which we proved by areas in Chapter 19, is built into barycentric coordinates — concurrency is a vanishing determinant. The coordinate system was designed around exactly the area-ratios Ceva measures. ■

Choosing your weapon

You now hold five computational languages. The skill is matching the tool to the problem.

Which bash?
  • Trigonometry — when angles and a circumcircle dominate (Law of Sines, 2R).
  • Cartesian coordinates — when there are perpendiculars, midpoints, or one or two circles; place axes to seed zeros.
  • Complex numbers — when rotations, equilateral triangles, or a single (unit) circle dominate.
  • Vectors — for midpoints, centroids, and dot-product perpendicularity, with full symmetry.
  • Barycentric — when the triangle’s own centres, cevians, and ratios are the whole story.
  • And always remember the synthetic option: the cleanest proof is often no bash at all.
✗ Common Trap

Bashing trades insight for certainty, and it can be long. Before committing, spend thirty seconds asking whether an angle chase, a spiral similarity, or one inversion would finish in three lines. Reach for coordinates when cleverness stalls — not before. And whichever engine you choose, define everything up front and check the answer against the diagram.

➤ Your turn

A triangle has sides a=5, b=6, c=7. Write the barycentric coordinates of its incentre, and find what fraction of the triangle’s area is [IBC].

Set-up (you finish it): the incentre is (a:b:c), and the first (normalised) coordinate is the area fraction a/(a+b+c).

Answer: incentre = (5:6:7); [IBC]/[ABC] = 5/(5+6+7) = 5/18.

Five languages for one geometry, and the quiet wisdom that the best move is sometimes to speak none of them and stay synthetic. A master is fluent in all of them, and loyal to none.

Key ideas & formulas
  • Barycentric coordinates: P = αA+βB+γC with α+β+γ=1; the triple is proportional to the areas [PBC]:[PCA]:[PAB].
  • The dictionary: centroid (1:1:1), incentre (a:b:c), circumcentre (a²(b²+c²−a²):···), orthocentre (tan A:tan B:tan C).
  • Cevian concurrency is a vanishing 3×3 determinant — Ceva is built in.
  • Choosing the bash: trig (angles, circumcircle), Cartesian (perpendiculars), complex (rotations, one circle), vectors (midpoints), barycentric (the triangle’s centres and ratios).
  • But stay synthetic when you can: the cleanest proof is often no bash at all.

Chapter 29How to Attack an Olympiad Problem

✦ Wonder

You sit down to a contest. Before you is a geometry problem you have never seen, with a statement of one or two lines and a blank page beneath. The clock is running. You know dozens of theorems — but which one, and where? The difference between the student who freezes and the one who finds the thread is not more theorems. It is method. What does a trained solver actually do in those first crucial minutes?

Every tool in this book is now in your hands. This chapter is about wielding them: the habits, the order of operations, and the inner monologue of a solver who meets a fresh problem and, step by step, takes it apart.

The five moves

  1. Draw it large and accurate. Use a ruler and compass; redraw if cramped. Mark every equal length and angle as you find them.
  2. State the goal precisely. An angle? A length or ratio? A concurrency or collinearity? A fixed point or locus?
  3. Match the goal to a tool. Angle / concyclic → chase, directed angles, tangent–chord. Length / ratio → similar triangles, sine & cosine, Stewart, power of a point. Concurrent / collinear → Ceva, Menelaus, radical axis, poles & polars. Stuck or symmetric → reflect, rotate, invert — or bash.
  4. Hunt the key claim. Work backwards from the goal; look for a hidden circle; add the one auxiliary line that links what you know to what you want.
  5. Write up every step. State each claim, justify it by name, and conclude. No “clearly.”

Two of these deserve emphasis. The diagram is not a sketch — it is your laboratory. A large, accurate figure reveals coincidences (three points that look collinear, four that look concyclic) which become the conjectures you then prove. And the auxiliary line — a parallel, a perpendicular, a circle, a reflection — is where most hard problems turn: the figure as given is a locked door, and the right extra line is the key.

A live solve

Watch the method in action. The narration is the part that matters.

☞ Worked Example

Problem. In triangle ABC, the incircle touches BC at X, and M is the midpoint of BC. Prove that the reflection of X over M is exactly where the A-excircle touches BC.

Move 1 — diagram. Draw a clearly scalene triangle, the incircle, X on BC, mark M.

Move 2 — goal. A statement about two lengths on BC being symmetric about M: show BX = CX′.

Move 3 — tool. Lengths on the sides with incircle/excircle: that is tangent lengths (Chapters 16, 24).

Move 4 — key claim. Recall BX = s−b. For the A-excircle, the tangent-length computation gives BX′ = s−c. So BX + BX′ = (s−b)+(s−c) = a = BC.

Move 5 — write-up. Since BX + BX′ = BC and both are measured from B along BC, the points X and X′ are equidistant from M on opposite sides: X′ is the reflection of X over M. ■

The takeaway: no brilliance was required — only the discipline to name the goal, recognise the configuration, and recall the right fact. That is what training buys: not magic, but a fast, reliable march from goal to tool to conclusion.

Aha!

When you are stuck, the productive questions are concrete: What have I not used? (every hypothesis must earn its place.) Do four points look concyclic? What if I drew the circle / the parallel / the reflection? Can I work backwards from the conclusion? Cycling through these — not staring harder — is how solvers get unstuck.

➤ Your turn

A problem asks you to prove that four given points are concyclic. Name two genuinely different methods you could reach for.

Set-up (you finish it): think about what “concyclic” converts into — an angle condition, or a length-product condition.

Answer: (1) an angle method — opposite angles sum to 180°, or equal angles in the same segment (directed-angle test ∠(CA,CB) = ∠(DA,DB)); (2) a power method — if AB, CD meet at P, show PA·PB = PC·PD (converse power of a point). A third: exhibit a centre equidistant from all four.

Method is the quiet engine under every brilliant solution. Drill the loop until it runs without you, and the blank page beneath the problem stops being a threat and becomes an invitation.

Key ideas & formulas
  • The five-move loop: (1) draw it large and accurate, marking equal lengths/angles; (2) state the goal precisely; (3) match goal to tool; (4) hunt the key claim; (5) write up every step — no “clearly.”
  • Goal → tool: angle/concyclic → chase, directed angles, tangent–chord; length/ratio → similar triangles, sine & cosine, Stewart, power of a point; concurrent/collinear → Ceva, Menelaus, radical axis, poles & polars; stuck/symmetric → reflect, rotate, invert, or bash.
  • The diagram is your laboratory: an accurate figure reveals the coincidences you then prove.
  • The auxiliary line (parallel, perpendicular, circle, reflection) is where most hard problems turn.
  • When stuck, ask: What have I not used? Do four points look concyclic? What if I drew the circle/parallel/reflection? Can I work backwards?
