Chapter 30The Summit: Olympiad Problems

✦ Wonder

Behind you stand every tool you have forged — angle chasing, the circle theorems, similarity and trigonometry, Ceva and Menelaus, transformations, inversion, the bash. None of them, alone, conquers a real olympiad problem. But together, summoned at the right instant, they do. One by one, watch each step onto the field at the exact moment it is needed.

Below are seven problems in the olympiad spirit, each solved in full — and each headlined by the tool that cracks it. Read the statement, cover the solution, and try the five-move loop yourself first. Then watch the tool do its work.

Problem 1 — Power of a Point

Two circles meet at A and B. A common tangent touches them at P and Q. Prove that line AB bisects PQ.

☞ Solution

Let M = AB ∩ PQ. Line AB is the radical axis of the two circles, so every point of it has equal power to both. At M, the power to the first circle is the squared tangent length MP², and to the second it is MQ². Equal powers give MP² = MQ², so MP = MQ: M is the midpoint of PQ. ■

Problem 2 — Inscribed Angles

Two circles meet at A and B. A variable line through A meets the first circle again at P and the second at Q. Prove that ∠PBQ is the same for every such line.

☞ Solution

P, A, Q are collinear, so ∠BPQ = ∠BPA and ∠BQP = ∠BQA. But ∠BPA is an inscribed angle in the first circle on the fixed chord BA — constant as P varies. Likewise ∠BQA is constant. In △PBQ, ∠PBQ = 180° − ∠BPA − ∠BQA, a sum of two constants. So ∠PBQ never changes. ■ (This constant angle is exactly the spiral similarity at B from one circle to the other.)

Problem 3 — The Tangent–Chord Angle

Two circles are tangent at T. A line through T meets one circle again at P and the other at Q. Prove the tangent to the first at P is parallel to the tangent to the second at Q.

☞ Solution

Let ℓ be the common tangent at T. In the first circle, the tangent–chord angle between ℓ and chord TP equals the angle the tangent at P makes with PT; the same holds at Q in the second. But both tangent–chord angles at T are the same angle, between ℓ and the common line PTQ. So the tangent at P and the tangent at Q make equal angles with line PQ on the same side — they are parallel. ■

Problem 4 — A 60° Rotation

Equilateral triangles ABF and ACG are erected outward on sides AB and AC of triangle ABC. Prove that BG = CF.

☞ Solution

Consider the rotation by 60° about A carrying F to B (it does, since AF = AB and ∠FAB = 60°). The same rotation carries C to G (since AC = AG and ∠CAG = 60°). So it sends segment FC to segment BG, and rotations preserve length: FC = BG. ■ (The same rotation shows BG and CF meet at 60° — the construction hides the Fermat point.)

Problem 5 — Inversion (Ptolemy’s Equality)

Prove that if ABCD is cyclic, then AC·BD = AB·CD + AD·BC.

☞ Solution

Invert about A with radius r. Since A, B, C, D are concyclic, the circle through them (passing through the centre A) inverts to a line; so B′, C′, D′ are collinear with C′ between, giving B′D′ = B′C′ + C′D′. Using X′Y′ = XY·r²/(AX·AY) and clearing denominators by AB·AC·AD/r²,

AC·BD = AD·BC + AB·CD. ■

Problem 6 — Euler’s Inequality

Prove that for every triangle, R ≥ 2r, with equality only for the equilateral triangle.

☞ Solution

The power of the incentre I with respect to the circumcircle is OI² − R²; computing it another way (it equals −2Rr) yields Euler’s formula OI² = R² − 2Rr. Since OI² ≥ 0, we get R² − 2Rr ≥ 0, i.e. R ≥ 2r. Equality holds exactly when OI = 0 — circumcentre and incentre coincide — which happens only for the equilateral triangle. ■

Problem 7 — A Configuration Capstone

Let H be the orthocentre of acute △ABC, and M the midpoint of BC. Prove that the reflection of H over M is the point A′ diametrically opposite A on the circumcircle.

☞ Solution

Let A′ be the antipode of A. Since AA′ is a diameter, ∠ABA′ = ∠ACA′ = 90°. So A′B ⊥ AB; but the altitude CH is also ⊥ AB, hence A′B ∥ CH. Likewise A′C ∥ BH. Therefore BHCA′ has both pairs of opposite sides parallel — a parallelogram. Its diagonals HA′ and BC bisect each other, so their common midpoint is M: A′ is the reflection of H over M. ■

Aha!

Look back over the seven. Not one needed a tool you do not own. Each fell to a single well-chosen idea — the radical axis, the inscribed angle, the alternate segment, a rotation, an inversion, Euler’s formula, a parallelogram — summoned at the right moment. That is the whole secret of olympiad geometry: not knowing more, but seeing which one, and trusting it. You can do this now.

Two true ascents

Each of the seven fell to a single idea. A real olympiad problem rarely does: it asks you to find several and chain them in an order nobody hands you. Here are two such climbs — and this time the write-up shows the search, not just the finished proof.

Ascent 1 — the lemma you will use most

Let I be the incentre of △ABC, and M the second point where the bisector of ∠A meets the circumcircle (the midpoint of arc BC not containing A). Prove that MB = MC = MI.

The hunt. We must tie I — a creature of angle bisectors — to the circumcircle. The bisector of ∠A already pierces the circle at M, so M is the natural bridge. One equality is free: M is the midpoint of arc BC, so equal arcs give equal chords, MB = MC. Everything rests on the strange claim MI = MB.

The pivot. First, A, I, M are collinear — all on the bisector of ∠A. To force MI = MB, aim to make △MBI isosceles, i.e. ∠MBI = ∠MIB. Split the angle at B: ∠MBI = ∠MBC + ∠CBI. The inscribed angles ∠MBC and ∠MAC stand on the same arc MC, so ∠MBC = ½∠A; and ∠CBI = ½∠B. Hence ∠MBI = ½∠A + ½∠B. For the other base angle, ∠MIB is the exterior angle of △ABI at I, so ∠MIB = ∠IAB + ∠IBA = ½∠A + ½∠B.

Thus ∠MBI = ∠MIB; triangle MBI is isosceles, and MI = MB = MC. ■ Three ideas had to arrive together — the arc-midpoint, the bisector, and the collinearity A I M — and the result is the single most-summoned lemma in olympiad geometry. Learn it, and half of every incentre problem swings open.

Ascent 2 — two circles, two tangents

Circles ω1 and ω2 meet at A and B. A line through A meets ω1 again at C and ω2 again at D. The tangent to ω1 at C and the tangent to ω2 at D meet at P. Prove that B, C, P, D lie on one circle.

The hunt. Two tangents should fire one reflex — the tangent–chord angle — and the goal, “four points concyclic,” is itself an angle statement. To dodge the configuration hazard, chase with directed angles (modulo 180°).

The chain. By the tangent–chord theorem in ω1, ∠(CP,CB) = ∠(AC,AB); in ω2, ∠(DP,DB) = ∠(AD,AB). Why should the right-hand sides agree? Because C, A, D are collinear — lines AC and AD are the same line. So ∠(CP,CB) = ∠(DP,DB), precisely the directed-angle test for B, C, P, D concyclic. ■

The tangent–chord theorem fired twice, the collinearity of C, A, D welded the halves together, and the directed-angle test closed the door — three tools, one chain, turning on the quiet observation that AC and AD are a single line.

➤ Your turn

Building straight on Problem 7: in acute △ABC with circumcentre O and orthocentre H, let M be the midpoint of BC. Prove that AH = 2·OM.

Set-up (you finish it): Problem 7 showed the antipode A′ of A is the reflection of H over M, so M is the midpoint of HA′; and O is the midpoint of AA′. Look at △AHA′ and the segment joining two midpoints.

Answer: in △AHA′, O is the midpoint of AA′ and M the midpoint of HA′, so OM is a midline: OM = ½AH, i.e. AH = 2·OM.
The whole arsenal, on one page
  • Angles: angle chasing & directed angles; inscribed-angle theorem, cyclic quadrilaterals, tangent–chord (alternate segment).
  • Lengths & circles: similar triangles; Law of Sines (=2R) & Cosines; area = ½ab sin C = abc/4R = rs; Stewart; power of a point; Ptolemy; the radical axis.
  • Concurrency / collinearity: Ceva, Menelaus (and trig forms), poles & polars, the cross-ratio.
  • Transformations: reflection, rotation, homothety, spiral similarity, inversion.
  • The bashes: coordinates, vectors, complex numbers, barycentrics — certainty when cleverness stalls.
  • The method: draw it large, name the goal, match it to a tool, hunt the key claim, write it up. The secret was never more tools — only seeing which one.

Return, if you like, to the folded square of the Prologue — the one hiding a 3–4–5 triangle. With coordinates, similar triangles, Pythagoras, and a reflection now in hand, write its proof. That problem was once impossible; today it is an exercise. That is how far you have climbed.

↑ Contents

EpilogueThe Garden in Bloom

Turn back, for a moment, to where we began.

A loop of knotted rope on the banks of the Nile. Twelve equal parts, pulled taut into a triangle of 3, 4, and 5 — and a perfect right angle, conjured from nothing but string. We did not know, then, why it worked. We only knew that it did, and that somewhere behind the trick lay a reason worth chasing.

Look how far that chase has carried you.

You began unable to define a point. You learned that mathematics is built not by defining everything, but by choosing where to stop — and from three undefined words you built the entire plane. You proved your first theorem, vertical angles, and felt the floor of certainty hold under your weight. You watched a triangle’s three angles, scattered and unequal, slide along one auxiliary line and fall into a perfect straight angle. The miracle was a straight line in disguise; you saw through it.

Then the tools began to gather, one by one, like a team assembling.

Congruence and similarity taught you when two figures are truly the same, and when they are merely echoes at different scales. Pythagoras arrived — and you met him not once but four times, because a truth seen from many sides is a truth you own. The triangle gave up its four hidden centres, and a single line — Euler’s — threaded three of them together as though they had been waiting all along.

You walked into the circle and found it was a machine for trading angles against lengths: the inscribed angle, frozen as a point slides along its arc; Ptolemy, binding the diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral to its sides; the power of a point, one number a point quietly remembers about a circle; the tangent, whispering across the circle through the alternate segment.

You assembled the toolbox. The angle chase, workhorse of them all. Trigonometry, where the Law of Sines turned out to be measuring the very circle through the triangle. Ceva and Menelaus, twins separated by a single sign. Coordinates, vectors, complex numbers — whole languages in which a rotation is just multiplication and a centroid is just an average. And transformations: the reflection that straightens a path, the 60° rotation that folded 3, 4, 5 into a single right angle at last.

And then the summit. The nine-point circle, nine coincidences collapsing into one scaling. The radical centre, conjured by pure transitivity. The spiral similarity, hiding at the crossing of two circles. Inversion, the great simplifier, turning circles into lines and making Ptolemy fall out of the humblest inequality there is.

Aha!

Here is the secret the whole book has been quietly teaching: olympiad geometry is not about knowing more theorems than the next person. It is about seeing — looking at a crowded, stubborn figure and recognising, in a heartbeat, which one idea will open it. That sight is not a gift you are born with. It is built, theorem by theorem, diagram by diagram, exactly as you have built it here.

The pentagram from the Prologue still hangs in the first pages, and the golden ratio still hides inside it. You could not reach it then. You can now. The folded square, the manhole cover that cannot fall through its own hole, the rope-stretchers’ triangle — every wonder we opened a chapter with is, today, an exercise you could finish before the tea goes cold.

So here is the truth the garden was always growing toward: you are the geometer now. The next time you face a figure no one has shown you — on a contest, on a blackboard, in your own notebook at midnight — you will not freeze. You will draw it large and true. You will name what you want. You will reach, without hesitation, for the one tool among many that fits. And the figure will open, the way the rope-stretchers’ right angle finally opened for you, because behind every beautiful coincidence there is a reason, and you have learned how to find it.

The road from a knotted cord to the International Mathematical Olympiad is long. You have just walked it. Whatever problem you meet next — harder, stranger, more beautiful — meet it the way you met every Wonder in this book: not with fear, but with the question that started everything.

Why?

— The Author

Appendix ATheorem & Formula Cheat-Sheet

A one-stop reference to every key result in the book. Use it to recall a fact fast; use the chapters to recall why.

Angles & triangles (Parts I–II)

  • Angles on a line sum to 180°; around a point, 360°; vertical angles are equal.
  • Across parallels: corresponding =, alternate =, co-interior sum 180°.
  • Triangle angle sum 180°; exterior angle = sum of the two remote interior angles.
  • Congruence: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS. Similarity: AA; areas scale as (ratio)².
  • Isosceles: equal sides face equal angles (and conversely).
  • Pythagoras a²+b²=c² and its converse.
  • Pythagorean triples: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (7,24,25), …

Centres & the Euler line (Ch. 10, 24)

  • Centroid G: medians, divides each 2:1; G = ⅓(A+B+C).
  • Circumcentre O (perp. bisectors), incentre I (angle bisectors, r = Area/s), orthocentre H (altitudes).
  • Euler line: O, G, H collinear, OG:GH = 1:2; with nine-point centre N, OG:GN:NH = 2:1:3.
  • Nine-point circle: N = midpoint OH, radius ½R; through 3 midpoints, 3 altitude-feet, 3 Euler points.
  • Euler: OI² = R² − 2Rr, hence R ≥ 2r.

Area (Ch. 11)

[T] = ½bh = ½ab sin C = abc4R = rs = s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c).

Shoelace: ½|x1(y2−y3) + x2(y3−y1) + x3(y1−y2)|.   Pick: Area = I + B/2 − 1.

The circle (Part III)

  • Inscribed angle = ½ central; same-segment angles equal; semicircle angle = 90°.
  • Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles sum 180° (and converse).
  • Ptolemy: AC·BD = AB·CD + AD·BC (equality iff cyclic; ≤ otherwise).
  • Power of a point = OP²−r²: chords PA·PB = PC·PD; tangent PT² = PA·PB.
  • Tangent ⊥ radius; two tangents from a point are equal; tangent–chord = alternate-segment inscribed angle.
  • Chord angle: inside = ½(arc+arc), outside = ½(arc−arc).

The toolbox (Part IV)

  • Law of Sines asin A = bsin B = csin C = 2R;   Law of Cosines c² = a²+b²−2ab cos C.
  • Ceva BDDC·CEEA·AFFB = 1 (concurrent); Menelaus = −1, signed (collinear).
  • Stewart b²m+c²n = a(d²+mn); median ma² = ¼(2b²+2c²−a²); bisector ta² = bc−BD·DC.
  • Distance (Δx)²+(Δy)²; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1; circle (x−h)²+(y−k)² = r².
  • Complex: ×eiθ rotates; equilateral ⇔ a²+b²+c² = ab+bc+ca. Vectors: →u·→v = 0 ⇔ ⊥.
  • Homothety ratio k scales lengths by |k|, areas by k²; spiral similarity multiplier (C−D)/(A−B).

Olympiad engines (Part V)

  • Radical centre: three radical axes concur; equal tangents from it.
  • Poles & polars: La Hire (P on polar of Q ⇔ Q on polar of P); cross-ratio is projection-invariant; harmonic = −1.
  • Spiral similarity centre = second intersection of circles (PAC), (PBD) where P = AB∩CD.
  • Inversion OP·OP′ = r²: lines ↔ circles through O; P′Q′ = PQ r²/(OP·OQ); conformal.
  • Barycentric: centroid (1:1:1), incentre (a:b:c); areal α:β:γ = [PBC]:[PCA]:[PAB].

↑ Contents

Appendix BConstructions

Every construction below uses only the straightedge and compass of Chapter 6. Each comes with its one-line justification — a construction is only as good as the proof that it works.

  • Perpendicular bisector of AB. Equal arcs from A and B meet at P, Q; draw PQ. (P, Q are equidistant from A, B.)
  • Midpoint of AB. The perpendicular bisector meets AB at its midpoint.
  • Bisector of an angle at A. Arc from A cuts the sides at P, Q; equal arcs from P, Q meet at R; draw AR. (△APR ≅ △AQR by SSS.)
  • Perpendicular to ℓ from a point P off it. Arc from P cuts ℓ at X, Y; the perpendicular bisector of XY passes through P.
  • Perpendicular to ℓ at a point P on it. Equal marks X, Y on either side of P, then the perpendicular bisector of XY.
  • Copy an angle onto a ray. Reproduce the arc and chord that define it. (SSS.)
  • Equilateral triangle on AB (Euclid I.1). Circles centred A (through B) and B (through A) meet at C. (All sides = AB, radii.)
  • 60°, 30°, 15° angles. Equilateral gives 60°; bisect for 30°, again for 15°.
  • 90°, 45° angles. Perpendicular gives 90°; bisect for 45°.
  • Parallel to ℓ through P. Copy the angle ℓ makes with a transversal, at P (equal corresponding angles).
  • Divide a segment into n equal parts. Mark n equal steps along an auxiliary ray from one end; connect and draw parallels (Basic Proportionality, Ch. 8).
  • Centre of a given circle. Two chords; their perpendicular bisectors meet at the centre.
  • Tangent from an external point P. Circle on diameter OP meets the given circle at the contact points (Thales: ∠OTP = 90°).
  • Circumcircle of △ABC. Two perpendicular bisectors give O; draw the circle through A.
  • Incircle of △ABC. Two angle bisectors give I; drop a perpendicular to a side for the radius.
  • n from a unit segment. Stack unit-height right triangles on growing hypotenuses — the spiral of Theodorus.
Known to be impossible

With straightedge and compass alone (proved with algebra in the 1800s): trisecting a general angle, doubling the cube, squaring the circle, and constructing a regular 7- or 9-gon. Knowing the limits is part of the craft.

Appendix CHints & Solutions

Hints, not full write-ups — the joy is in finishing them yourself. A hint should be just enough to get unstuck.

Selected Olympiad Sparks

  • Ch. 4, the pentagram. Each star-point angle is an inscribed angle; the five subtend, between them, the whole circle once. The five total ½·360° = 180°.
  • Ch. 5, ∠EAF = 45° in a square. Rotate △ABE by 90° about A so AB→AD; the images of E, F, D become collinear, and EF = BE+DF drops out.
  • Ch. 9, P inside an equilateral, PA=3, PB=4, PC=5. Rotate 60° about a vertex to build a 3–4–5 right angle; the side is 25+123.
  • Ch. 14, sine addition via Ptolemy. In a unit-diameter circle a chord on inscribed angle θ has length sin θ; apply Ptolemy to the cyclic quadrilateral.
  • Ch. 18, tan A+tan B+tan C = tan A tan B tan C. Use C = 180°−(A+B) and the tangent addition formula.
  • Ch. 22 & 30, equilaterals on two sides. One 60° rotation about A carries F→B and C→G, so CF→BG.

The “twenty more” (Chapter 30)

  • 3. Both the ∠A-bisector and the perpendicular bisector of BC pass through the midpoint of arc BC not containing A.
  • 4 (Simson). P and two feet see a side at 90°, giving cyclic quadrilaterals; a short directed-angle chase forces the three feet collinear.
  • 7. Rotate 90° about B (so A↦C); a 1–22–3 right triangle appears and ∠APB = 135°.
  • 8 (Newton–Gauss). Stage 1: a complete quadrilateral is four lines; its three diagonals join the three pairs of “opposite” intersection points. Stage 2: write each diagonal’s midpoint as the average of its endpoints (position vectors). Stage 3: show one midpoint is an affine combination of the other two — a single linear relation — so the three are collinear.
  • 12 (symmedian). The tangents at B, C meet at the pole of BC; tangent–chord angles show it lies on the reflection of the median over the ∠A-bisector.
  • 13 (mixtilinear). Its centre lies on the ∠A-bisector, so the touch points P, Q on AB, AC are symmetric across that bisector and PQ ⊥ the bisector; prove I is the midpoint of PQ. (Hard.)
  • 15. Use cos A+cos B+cos C = 1 + 4 sin(A/2) sin(B/2) sin(C/2) and r = 4R sin(A/2) sin(B/2) sin(C/2).
  • 16 (Feuerbach). Stage 1: incircle (centre I, radius r) and nine-point circle (centre N, radius ½R) are internally tangent exactly when NI = ½R−r — that single equation is the whole target. Stage 2: place N as the midpoint of OH and compute NI² using Euler’s OI² = R²−2Rr. Stage 3: simplify to NI = ½R−r. (One of geometry’s gems.)
  • 17 (Descartes). Stage 1: invert at a tangency of two of the four circles; those two become parallel lines, the other two equal circles between them. Stage 2: in that strip the curvature relation is nearly visible. Stage 3: invert back, tracking each curvature, to reach (k1+k2+k3+k4)² = 2(k1²+k2²+k3²+k4²).
  • 18. The four Euler lines pass through the anticentre of the cyclic quadrilateral.
  • 20. Fix a chord and slide the third vertex (Ch. 11’s equal-area idea) to see each adjustment toward equilateral increases the area; iterate, or apply Jensen to sin.

The capstone: the folded square, proved

The Prologue promised a proof “when you are a master.” Here it is. Place the unit square with A=(0,0), B=(1,0), C=(1,1), D=(0,1), and fold corner C onto M=(½,0), the midpoint of the non-adjacent side AB.

The crease is the perpendicular bisector of CM. A short computation places it as the line y = −½x+⅞, meeting the right edge BC at E=(1,⅜); reflecting edge CD across the crease, its image meets the left edge AD at G=(0,⅔).

The right-hand triangle. Because E lies on the crease, the fold gives EM=EC. Writing BE=e (so EC=1−e), the right triangle BEM (right angle at B) has legs BE=e, BM=½ and hypotenuse EM=1−e. Pythagoras gives e²+¼ = (1−e)², hence e=⅜, and

BE : BM : EM = ⅜ : ½ : ⅝ = 3 : 4 : 5.

The other two. The fold sends the right angle of the square at C to a right angle at M, so the three triangles strung along the base AB are right-angled at A, M, B — and each works out to 3:4:5:

△AMG: ½, ⅔, ⅚ = 3:4:5;   △GME: ⅝, ⅚, 25/24 = 3:4:5;   △BEM: 3:4:5.

Each is similar to the rope-stretchers’ triangle. The motif that opened the book closes in four lines of algebra. ■

Mathematician’s Margin

For the unstarred problems, the relevant chapter’s main theorem is the intended tool — and the Cheat-Sheet (Appendix A) will point you to it. Resist looking; a problem you crack yourself is worth ten you are shown.

Appendix DFurther Reading

You have finished the journey of this book. Here is how to keep climbing.

Books to grow with

  • Coxeter & Greitzer, Geometry Revisited. The classic next step — elegant, deep, and humane. Read it slowly.
  • Evan Chen, Euclidean Geometry in Mathematical Olympiads (EGMO). The modern standard; directed angles, configurations, and a superb problem set.
  • Yaglom, Geometric Transformations (I–IV). Everything reflections, rotations, and inversion can do, taught through problems.
  • Honsberger, Episodes in Nineteenth and Twentieth Century Euclidean Geometry. Beautiful results, gently told.
  • Johnson, Advanced Euclidean Geometry. An encyclopaedic reference for the triangle’s hidden riches.
  • Posamentier & Salkind, Challenging Problems in Geometry. A large, friendly bank of problems with solutions.

The competition ladder

Geometry lives inside the wider olympiad movement. A typical path:

  • United States: AMC 10/12 → AIME → USA(J)MO → MOP → IMO.
  • India: IOQM → RMO → INMO → IMO Training Camp → IMO.
  • Most countries run a similar funnel of national rounds feeding the International Mathematical Olympiad.

Whatever your country, the engine is the same: a national body selects, through escalating rounds, a team of six for the IMO each July.

How to practise

  • Solve past papers, untimed at first, then timed. Olympiad archives are freely available online.
  • Write full solutions. A problem is not finished until your write-up has no “clearly.” Graders reward rigour.
  • Keep a key-claim log (Chapter 29): for each problem, record the one idea that cracked it. Patterns will emerge.
  • Read others’ solutions after you have tried hard — communities like the Art of Problem Solving forums are a treasure.
  • Draw, always. A large, accurate diagram remains your sharpest tool.

A last word

Talent helps, but it is wildly overrated next to patience, curiosity, and the habit of finishing what you start. Every olympian was once a beginner who could not define a point — and who kept asking why. You now carry the whole toolkit of Euclidean geometry, the discipline to deploy it, and the taste to find the elegant path. The rest is mileage, and mileage is just time spent doing something you have come to love.

Go find a hard, beautiful problem. Draw it large. And begin.

The garden is yours. Tend it well.
